## Section 5: Diversity — H2 {.page-break-before}

:::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
H2 predicts higher summer alpha diversity, tracking the richer summer diet. Two levels of analysis are presented together deliberately, because they appear to disagree in an informative way: the **pooled-season** estimate of 5.1 (which pools samples within a Season and asks about the Season's total species pool) versus the **per-sample** estimate of 5.2 (which asks about diversity within a single dropping and rewards evenness). Both are computed with iNEXT3D, so the disagreement cannot be an artefact of using two different estimators — 5.1 standardises by coverage across the two pooled incidence sets, 5.2 standardises by size across the 52 individual samples. The disagreement is resolved by the dominance analysis in 5.3.
::::

H2 predicts higher summer alpha diversity. It is assessed at two levels that give opposite answers: the diversity of each season's pooled droppings (Section 5.1) and the diversity within single droppings (Section 5.2). Both are estimated with iNEXT3D, so the difference is not an artefact of the estimator; Section 5.3 shows that it comes from dominance.

Per-sample Hill numbers are size-standardised to a common depth of 12,615 reads — the minimum library size — using `iNEXT.3D::estimate3D(base = "size")` on the raw counts. This returns the analytic expectation of the Hill number at that depth, rather than the value observed in one random rarefaction draw, so the estimate is deterministic and uses the full read depth of every sample. Coverage-based standardisation is **not** used at the per-sample level: estimated sample coverage is ≥ 0.99999 in all 52 samples (exactly 1 in 46 of them, since 43 contain no singleton OTUs at all), which leaves coverage-based and asymptotic estimators either undefined or equal to the observed richness, and would reintroduce the dependence on sequencing depth that standardisation is there to remove.

### 5.1 iNEXT3D: coverage-based taxonomic diversity

Incidence (presence in a dropping) depends on read depth, and summer libraries are about 2.6 times deeper than winter ones (median 551,236 vs 209,602 reads). The pooled comparison is therefore made with depth held equal: every sample is rarefied to the canonical minimum of 12,615 reads before the incidence matrices are built, both Seasons are compared at one common sample coverage (0.65), and the whole procedure is repeated over 50 independent rarefaction draws. Table S8 reports the median over draws of each estimate and of its bootstrap 95% CI. Asymptotic (extrapolated) estimates are not used for inference, because with 26 droppings per Season they extrapolate to roughly twice the observed richness.

![](figures/H2_iNEXT_TD_by_Season_rarefied.png)

**Figure S7**: iNEXT3D coverage-based rarefaction/extrapolation of taxonomic Hill numbers (q = 0, 1, 2), samples pooled within each Season (incidence data, nboot = 200), after rarefying every sample to 12,615 reads. The curves are drawn for the one rarefaction draw whose summer/winter ratio at q = 0 is closest to the median over 50 draws. Summer exceeds winter at every q.

```{r tab-inext}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
s8 <- read.csv("tables/H2_iNEXT3D_TD_coverage_rarefied.csv", check.names = FALSE)
kable(data.frame(
  Season = s8$Season, q = s8$Order.q,
  `Estimate` = round(s8$qTD, 1),
  `95% CI` = sprintf("%.1f–%.1f", s8$qTD.LCL, s8$qTD.UCL),
  `Summer/winter` = ifelse(s8$Season == "Summer",
                           sprintf("%.2f (%.2f–%.2f)", s8$ratio_summer_winter_median,
                                   s8$ratio_draw_2.5, s8$ratio_draw_97.5), ""),
  `Draws with separated CIs` = ifelse(s8$Season == "Summer",
                                      sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * s8$share_draws_CI_separated), ""),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Table S8. Pooled-season taxonomic Hill diversity at equal sequencing depth and equal sample coverage (iNEXT3D, incidence data; every sample rarefied to 12,615 reads; coverage 0.65; 50 rarefaction draws, 100 bootstraps each). Estimate and CI are medians over draws. 'Summer/winter' is the median ratio of the two estimates with the 2.5–97.5% range across draws. The last column is the share of draws in which the two Seasons' 95% CIs do not overlap.")
```

The summer/winter ratios of Table S8 are main-text **Fig. 4A** (Section 10.4), with an interval taken over every rarefaction draw × bootstrap replicate (`tables/H2_iNEXT3D_TD_coverage_rarefied_boot.csv`); the season estimates themselves are drawn in Figure S8b(A) (Section 5.5). Summer is the richer pooled assemblage at every order, by a factor of 1.42 at q = 0, 1.57 at q = 1 and 1.78 at q = 2.

:::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
**Raw-count and asymptotic versions (superseded as the primary result).** Without rarefying first, the same coverage-standardised comparison gives summer/winter ratios of 1.73, 1.96 and 2.28 (`tables/H2_iNEXT3D_TD_coverage_standardised.csv`), i.e. about a fifth of the raw summer advantage is the depth difference. The asymptotic estimates below were the Table S8 of earlier drafts; they carry the same depth confound and extrapolate to about twice the observed richness (summer 1,708 vs 864 observed; winter 1,046 vs 436), which is the regime in which asymptotic richness is least reliable.

![](figures/H2_iNEXT_TD_by_Season.png)

```{r tab-inext-asy}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
inx <- read.csv("tables/H2_iNEXT3D_TD_asymptotic.csv", check.names = FALSE)
kable(inx, digits = 2,
      caption = "Table S8b. iNEXT3D asymptotic taxonomic-diversity estimates by Season on raw (unrarefied) incidence (Hill q = 0, 1, 2; observed and asymptotic, with s.e. and 95% CI). Not used for inference.")
```
::::

### 5.2 Per-sample Hill diversity

![](figures/H2_hill_boxplot_Season.png)

**Figure S8**: Per-sample Hill numbers (PCR-collapsed object, size-standardised with iNEXT3D to the minimum sample depth of 12,615 reads). Winter exceeds summer at q1/q2 (Shannon/Simpson); summer has the higher mean at q0 (richness), but that difference is weak and depends on the model family (Tables S9, S9b).

Figure S8b(B) (Section 5.5) redraws the same quantity annotated with the Table S9 contrasts below and stacked beneath the pooled estimates on a shared set of facet columns, and main-text **Fig. 4A** (Section 10.4) plots the Table S9 ratios themselves. Figure S8 is retained here as the plain, unannotated view.

The Season effect is tested on the plotted values themselves: one size-standardised value per dung sample (n = 52), with a gamma GLM (log link) of `q ~ Season + Year`, so the Season coefficient is a summer/winter ratio adjusted for year. Year is a fixed effect (three levels are too few to estimate a variance), and individual bird is not modelled because only three birds were sampled more than once. The Season × Year interaction is tested by F-test and ΔAICc against the additive model.

```{r tab-lmm}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
s9 <- read.csv("tables/H2_season_effect_per_sample.csv", check.names = FALSE)
pf <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, "< 0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p))
kable(data.frame(
  q = s9$metric, n = s9$n,
  `Mean winter` = round(s9$mean_winter, 1), `Mean summer` = round(s9$mean_summer, 1),
  `Summer/winter (95% CI)` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f–%.2f)", s9$ratio_summer_winter,
                                     s9$ratio_lwr, s9$ratio_upr),
  `F (Season)` = round(s9$F_season, 2), `p (Season)` = pf(s9$p_season),
  `p (Year)` = pf(s9$p_year), `p (Season × Year)` = pf(s9$p_season_x_year),
  `ΔAICc (interaction)` = round(s9$dAICc_interaction, 1),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Table S9. Season effect on per-sample Hill diversity (gamma GLM, log link, q ~ Season + Year; n = 52 dung samples, size-standardised to 12,615 reads). The ratio is summer/winter adjusted for year, with a Wald 95% CI; p-values are F-tests. The Season × Year interaction is tested against the additive model; positive ΔAICc means the interaction is not supported.")
```

```{r tab-lmm-family}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
s9b <- read.csv("tables/H2_season_effect_family_sensitivity.csv", check.names = FALSE)
pf <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, "< 0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p))
kable(data.frame(
  q = s9b$metric,
  Gaussian = pf(s9b$p_gaussian), `Log-normal` = pf(s9b$p_lognormal),
  `Gamma (Table S9)` = pf(s9b$p_gamma), `Wilcoxon (unadjusted)` = pf(s9b$p_wilcoxon),
  `AIC Gaussian` = round(s9b$AIC_gaussian, 1), `AIC log-normal` = round(s9b$AIC_lognormal, 1),
  `AIC gamma` = round(s9b$AIC_gamma, 1),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Table S9b. Sensitivity of the Season test to the error family (Season p-value, same Season + Year model; Wilcoxon rank-sum without Year). AIC is on the response scale; the log-normal value includes the Jacobian term so it is comparable with the others.")
```

:::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
The two abundance-weighted orders are unambiguous: a winter dropping holds about 2.2 times (q = 1) and 2.5 times (q = 2) the effective number of OTUs of a summer one, under every family (p ≤ 0.005) and in every year (no Season × Year interaction). Richness (q = 0) is not: summer's mean is higher (48.3 vs 31.3 OTUs at equal depth), but the difference is significant only under the gamma model (p = 0.026, the AIC-preferred family for q = 0) and not under the Gaussian (p = 0.063), log-normal (p = 0.29) or rank-based (p = 0.11) tests. It is carried by a minority of very rich summer samples (summer median 35.6 vs winter 25.8).
::::

:::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
**Replicate-level model (superseded as Table S9).** Earlier drafts tested Season with linear mixed models on PCR replicates (n = 98, each replicate size-standardised to 10,609 reads) with random intercepts for dung sample and, where estimable, Year and individual bird, dropping terms that went singular. That fitted a different unit and depth from the one plotted, and used a different random-effects structure at q = 0 (Year dropped after singular fits) than at q = 1–2. Retained for reference:

```{r tab-lmm-pcr}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
lmm <- read.csv("tables/H2_lmm_season_effect.csv", check.names = FALSE)
kable(lmm, digits = 3,
      caption = "Table S9c. Replicate-level mixed-model Season effect (summer minus winter) on per-replicate Hill diversity, with 95% CI and p. Superseded by Table S9.")
```
::::

### 5.3 Why the two metrics disagree: dominance and evenness

Pooling a Season's samples rewards the total species list (summer's samples collectively contain more species, so summer wins at every q). Per-sample q1/q2 instead downweight rare taxa and reward *within-sample evenness* — and individual summer samples are far more dominance-skewed than winter ones, so a single summer sample's effective diversity is lower even where its species list is longer.

```{r tab-dominance}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
dom <- read.csv("tables/report_dominance_summary.csv", check.names = FALSE)
names(dom) <- c("Season", "n", "Mean richness (q0, 12,615 reads)", "Mean top-1 OTU share (%)",
                "Mean Pielou J", "Wilcoxon p (richness)",
                "Wilcoxon p (top-1 share)", "Wilcoxon p (evenness J)")
kable(dom, digits = 3,
      caption = "Table S10. Per-sample richness, top-1-OTU dominance, and Pielou evenness by Season, with Wilcoxon tests (canonical object, 52 samples). Richness is size-standardised to 12,615 reads (the q0 of Figure S8), because summer libraries are about 2.6 times deeper; top-1 share is a proportion and does not depend on depth, and Pielou J agrees with a size-standardised evenness, ln(q1)/ln(q0), at r = 0.995.")
```

:::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
Concretely: a summer sample's single most abundant OTU accounts for **56%** of its reads on average (vs **25%** in winter, p \< 0.001), and Pielou evenness is correspondingly much lower (J = 0.38 summer vs 0.72 winter, p \< 0.001). Summer's pooled species list is longer (the long tail iNEXT3D detects across droppings), while within a dropping one or two OTUs dominate the read count — evenness collapses, and q1/q2 track evenness more than richness.
::::

### 5.4 Which OTUs dominate each Season?

```{r tab-top5}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
top5 <- read.csv("tables/report_top5_otu_by_season.csv", check.names = FALSE)
clean_tax <- function(v) ifelse(is.na(v) | v == "", "—", sub("^[a-z]__", "", v))
top5$Season  <- tools::toTitleCase(top5$Season)
top5$Order   <- clean_tax(top5$Order)
top5$Genus   <- clean_tax(top5$Genus)
top5$Species <- clean_tax(top5$Species)
top5 <- top5[, c("Season", "OTU", "mean_pct_share", "Order", "Genus", "Species")]
names(top5) <- c("Season", "OTU", "Mean % share (within-season)", "Order", "Genus", "Species")
kable(top5, digits = 2,
      caption = "Table S11. Top-5 dominant OTUs per Season by mean within-season read share, with taxonomy.")
```

Summer's dominance is driven by three strongly season-skewed OTUs: **OTU1 (*Thelebolus*)** averages 24.9% of summer reads (15/26 summer samples vs 5/26 winter at 3.2%), **OTU1225 (*Coniochaeta*)** is essentially summer-only (10.1% vs 0.2%), and **OTU636 (*Sporormiella* cf. *intermedia*)** is also summer-skewed (9.0% vs 2.5%). Winter's own top OTU, **OTU1369**, is a "dark taxon" (unclassified below Class, Dothideomycetes), present in 20/26 winter samples but only 3/26 summer, at 11.2% mean winter share.

```{r sec5-build}
#| eval: false
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for Tables S10, S11 and S3 (dominance and evenness, top-5 OTUs, coprophilous screen) — the source of truth for those three tables"

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Sections 5.3-5.4 and Table S3 (Section 3.2): per-sample dominance and
# evenness, the top-5 OTUs of each Season, and the coprophilous-genus screen.
#
# This chunk is the source of truth for those three tables; there is no
# parallel script. Tables S8-S9 and Figures S7-S8 (Sections 5.1-5.2) are
# produced by Scripts/6_diversity_analyses.R Sections 1-2 (see the pointer
# chunk above); the size-standardised per-sample Hill numbers used below for
# Table S10 richness are read from the table that script stages, not
# recomputed here.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
library(phyloseq); library(dplyr)

data_dir <- "/home/daniel/Ptarmigan/trimmed/mergedPlates"   # data live outside the repo
tab_dir  <- "tables"                                        # relative to this .qmd
load(file.path(data_dir, "eco_analysis.RData"))

# Per-sample Hill numbers (Figure S8), size-standardised to 12,615 reads by
# Scripts/6_diversity_analyses.R Section 2.
hill_sample <- read.csv(file.path(tab_dir, "H2_hill_per_sample.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# ===========================================================================
# Table S10 -- dominance and evenness, per sample
# ===========================================================================
ps <- alldat$nopool
otu_mat <- as(otu_table(ps), "matrix")
if (!taxa_are_rows(ps)) otu_mat <- t(otu_mat)      # taxa x samples
sd <- as.data.frame(sample_data(ps))
stopifnot(identical(colnames(otu_mat), rownames(sd)))
rel_mat <- sweep(otu_mat, 2, colSums(otu_mat), "/")

pielou_J <- function(p) { p <- p[p > 0]; (-sum(p * log(p))) / log(length(p)) }

# Richness is the SIZE-STANDARDISED q0 of Figure S8 (12,615 reads), not the raw
# OTU count: summer libraries are ~2.6x deeper, so raw counts compare unequal
# effort. The raw count is kept in the per-sample CSV for reference only.
# Pielou J stays on the raw counts: checked against the size-standardised
# evenness ln(q1)/ln(q0), r = 0.995 across samples and the same seasonal contrast
# (0.41 vs 0.75, Wilcoxon p ~ 1e-7), so depth does not drive it.
hs_i <- match(colnames(otu_mat), hill_sample$sample); stopifnot(!anyNA(hs_i))
dom_df <- data.frame(
  sample = colnames(otu_mat), Season = sd$Season, Year = sd$Year,
  richness  = hill_sample$q0[hs_i],
  richness_observed_raw = colSums(otu_mat > 0),
  top1_prop = apply(rel_mat, 2, max),
  pielou_J  = apply(rel_mat, 2, pielou_J),
  evenness_size_std = log(hill_sample$q1[hs_i]) / log(hill_sample$q0[hs_i]),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

season_summary <- dom_df %>% group_by(Season) %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean_richness      = round(mean(richness), 1),
            mean_top1_prop_pct = round(100 * mean(top1_prop), 1),
            mean_pielou_J      = round(mean(pielou_J), 2), .groups = "drop")

wilcox_rich <- wilcox.test(richness  ~ Season, data = dom_df)
wilcox_top1 <- wilcox.test(top1_prop ~ Season, data = dom_df)
wilcox_J    <- wilcox.test(pielou_J  ~ Season, data = dom_df)

write.csv(dom_df, file.path(tab_dir, "report_dominance_per_sample.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(season_summary %>%
            mutate(wilcox_p_richness  = round(wilcox_rich$p.value, 5),
                   wilcox_p_top1_prop = round(wilcox_top1$p.value, 5),
                   wilcox_p_pielou_J  = round(wilcox_J$p.value, 5)),
          file.path(tab_dir, "report_dominance_summary.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

# ===========================================================================
# Table S11 -- top-5 dominant OTUs per Season
# ===========================================================================
tax <- as.data.frame(as(tax_table(ps), "matrix"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
seasons <- levels(factor(sd$Season))
top5_df <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(seasons, function(s) {
  shares   <- rowMeans(rel_mat[, rownames(sd)[sd$Season == s], drop = FALSE])
  top5_ids <- names(sort(shares, decreasing = TRUE))[1:5]
  data.frame(Season = s, OTU = top5_ids,
             mean_pct_share = round(100 * shares[top5_ids], 2),
             tax[top5_ids, c("Phylum", "Class", "Order", "Family", "Genus", "Species")],
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}))
write.csv(top5_df, file.path(tab_dir, "report_top5_otu_by_season.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

# ===========================================================================
# Table S3 (Section 3.2) -- coprophilous-genus screen
# ===========================================================================
# ONE list, used for both Table S3 and the Season test below: recognised
# coprophilous genera, including Thelebolus and Coniochaeta, which carry the
# seasonal signal in this dataset (Sections 5.4, 6.2, 8.2). It is the
# project's single canonical list -- identical to COPRO_GENERA in scripts 6, 7,
# 8 and 10 and in the fig1-build / fig4-build chunks; change them together.
COPRO_GENERA <- c("Sordaria","Podospora","Cercophora","Chaetomium","Schizothecium",
                  "Preussia","Delitschia","Pilobolus","Ascobolus","Saccobolus",
                  "Sporormiella","Coprinopsis","Thelebolus","Coniochaeta")

# UNITE taxonomy carries rank prefixes ("g__Thelebolus"); strip them or the
# %in% match silently fails. "unidentified" placeholders become NA.
strip_pref <- function(x) {
  x <- ifelse(is.na(x), NA_character_, sub("^[a-z]__", "", x))
  x[x == "" | grepl("unidentified", x, ignore.case = TRUE)] <- NA
  x
}
genus_clean <- strip_pref(tax$Genus)
copro_flag  <- !is.na(genus_clean) & genus_clean %in% COPRO_GENERA
copro_otus  <- rownames(tax)[copro_flag]

w <- sd$Season == "winter"; s <- sd$Season == "summer"
copro_by_otu <- data.frame(
  OTU     = copro_otus,
  Genus   = genus_clean[copro_flag],
  Species = strip_pref(tax$Species[copro_flag]),
  winter_mean_pct = round(100 * rowMeans(rel_mat[copro_otus, w, drop = FALSE]), 3),
  summer_mean_pct = round(100 * rowMeans(rel_mat[copro_otus, s, drop = FALSE]), 3),
  occ_winter = rowSums(rel_mat[copro_otus, w, drop = FALSE] > 0),
  occ_summer = rowSums(rel_mat[copro_otus, s, drop = FALSE] > 0),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
copro_by_otu <- copro_by_otu[order(-(copro_by_otu$winter_mean_pct +
                                     copro_by_otu$summer_mean_pct)), ]
write.csv(copro_by_otu, file.path(tab_dir, "report_coprophilous_by_season_v2.csv"),
          row.names = FALSE)

# Per-sample total coprophilous read share, and the Season test quoted in
# Section 3.2 -- same COPRO_GENERA list as Table S3 above.
copro_df <- data.frame(sample = colnames(rel_mat), Season = sd$Season,
                       copro_pct_share = 100 * colSums(rel_mat[copro_otus, , drop = FALSE]))
print(copro_df %>% group_by(Season) %>%
        summarise(mean_pct = round(mean(copro_pct_share), 2),
                  median_pct = round(median(copro_pct_share), 2), .groups = "drop"))
print(wilcox.test(copro_pct_share ~ Season, data = copro_df))
```


### 5.5 Summary figure: pooled versus per-sample diversity

![](figures/S8b_richness_evenness_crossover.png)

**Figure S8b**: The summer dung mycobiome holds more fungal OTUs than winter ones, yet each individual dropping is far less even. **(A)** Taxonomic diversity of each season's pooled sample set (iNEXT3D, incidence data) at Hill orders q = 0, 1 and 2 at equal sequencing depth. Points are the median estimate over 50 rarefaction draws, and bars the median 95% CI. **(B)** Per-sample Hill numbers for the same 52 samples, size-standardised to 12,615 reads. Boxes show the median and interquartile range, points are individual samples, white diamonds are season means, and the grey segment joins those means. Annotations give the year-adjusted summer/winter ratio with its p-value from the GLMs of Table S9. **(C)** Per-sample top-1-OTU read share and Pielou evenness J, both on a 0–1 scale, with symbols as in (B) and brackets giving the Wilcoxon rank-sum result (Table S10). **(D)** The identity of the dominants: the five OTUs with the highest mean within-season read share in each season, coloured by functional guild. Bar labels give that mean share and, in parentheses, the number of the season's 26 samples in which the OTU was detected at all. Taxa are named at the finest confidently assigned rank.

:::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
*This was main-text Figure 4 until 2026-11; main-text Figure 4 (Section 10.4) now shows the summer/winter ratios of panels A and B and the top-1 OTU share of panel C.*

**Figure S8b (full legend)**: The summer dung mycobiome is the richer assemblage when droppings are pooled, yet each individual dropping is far less even. **(A)** Taxonomic diversity of each season's pooled sample set at Hill orders q = 0, 1 and 2, at equal sequencing depth (every sample rarefied to 12,615 reads) and equal sample coverage (0.65) (iNEXT3D, incidence data); points are the median estimate over 50 rarefaction draws, bars the median 95% confidence interval, and the grey segment joins the two seasons within an order. Summer exceeds winter at every order (Table S8). **(B)** Per-sample Hill numbers for the same 52 samples, size-standardised with iNEXT3D to a common depth of 12,615 reads, drawn in the same three columns against the same season axis so that the two rows can be read against one another; boxes show the median and interquartile range, points are individual samples, white diamonds are season means, and the grey segment joins those means. The slope that rises in all three columns of (A) rises only at q = 0 here and falls at q = 1 and q = 2 — that reversal is the crossover. Annotations give the year-adjusted summer/winter ratio and its p-value from a gamma GLM fitted to the plotted per-sample values (Table S9); the q = 0 contrast depends on the model family (p = 0.026–0.29; Table S9b), the q = 1 and q = 2 contrasts do not. Both rows scale y freely within each column, because the three Hill orders differ by an order of magnitude. **(C)** The mechanism: per-sample top-1-OTU read share and Pielou evenness *J*, both on a 0–1 scale, with symbols as in (B) and brackets giving the Wilcoxon rank-sum result (Table S10). **(D)** The identity of the dominants — the five OTUs with the highest mean within-season read share in each season, coloured by functional guild under the rule of Section 8.1. Bar labels give that mean share and, in parentheses, the number of the season's 26 samples in which the OTU was detected at all. Taxa are named at the finest confidently assigned rank, so an OTU with no genus appears under its family, or as *unclassified* plus its order or class. *Candida parapsilosis* is coloured plant-associated because its compound FUNGuild string contains `Epiphyte`; the rule is applied unchanged rather than special-cased, so that Figures 1 and 4 and Sections 8–9 classify every OTU identically.

Panels A and B put the same question to two scales and get opposite answers, and that disagreement is the result rather than a problem with it. Pooled across a season and with sequencing depth held equal, summer is the richer assemblage at every Hill order — 548 against winter's 383 OTUs at q = 0, and the gap widens under abundance weighting (412 vs 261 at q = 1; 287 vs 162 at q = 2). Within a single dropping the ordering reverses as soon as abundance enters: winter droppings are significantly more diverse at q = 1 (14.9 vs 7.4 effective OTUs; summer/winter 0.46, p = 0.001) and q = 2 (10.1 vs 4.6; 0.40, p < 0.001), whereas at q = 0 summer's higher mean (48.3 vs 31.3) is a weak, family-dependent difference carried by a few very rich summer samples (Tables S9, S9b). Panel C locates the reversal in dominance rather than in the species lists: an average summer sample gives 56% of its reads to a single OTU against 25% in winter, and Pielou evenness falls from 0.72 to 0.38 (both p \< 0.001). Summer droppings are far more top-heavy, which is precisely what depresses q = 1 and q = 2 even where a dropping's species list is as long as, or longer than, a winter one. Panel D names the taxa responsible, and they are the ones a coprophilous account predicts: *Thelebolus*, *Coniochaeta* and *Sporormiella intermedia* together take 44% of summer reads and are all dung saprotrophs, whereas winter's leading OTUs are mostly unclassified below class and carry no guild call at all — among them OTU1369, an unclassified Dothideomycete that is winter's most abundant OTU and is present in 20 of 26 winter samples, and which is taken up as a dark taxon in Section 3.4. Two caveats travel with the figure. The per-sample richness contrast in (B) is not robust to the choice of model family (Table S9b), so the crossover is firm at q = 1 and q = 2 and in the pooled estimates of (A), but not as a per-dropping richness gain. And the shares in (D) are seasonal averages, not universals — *Thelebolus* reaches its 24.9% mean while being detected in only 15 of the 26 summer droppings.
::::

```{r figS8b-build}
#| eval: false
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Build code for Figure S8b — source of truth for figures/S8b_richness_evenness_crossover.{png,pdf}"

# Figure S8b -- the four-panel H2 summary that was main-text Figure 4 until
# 2026-11, carried over verbatim (only the output name changed): A pooled-season
# iNEXT3D estimates (Table S8), B per-sample size-standardised Hill numbers with the
# Table S9 contrasts, C dominance and evenness (Table S10), D top-5 OTUs per season
# (Table S11). Per-sample quantities are recomputed via hill_size_helper.R; pooled
# estimates and test statistics are READ from committed tables/ CSVs, with guards.
# Rebuild:  conda run -n r_env Rscript build_main_figure.R figS8b-build


suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(phyloseq); library(ggplot2); library(patchwork); library(iNEXT.3D)
})
# Size-standardised Hill numbers: the same estimator Scripts/6_diversity_analyses.R
# uses for Section 5.2 (it carries a verbatim copy); the guard below checks the
# season means against the table that script writes.
source("hill_size_helper.R")

rdata <- if (file.exists("eco_analysis.RData")) "eco_analysis.RData" else
         "/home/daniel/Ptarmigan/trimmed/mergedPlates/eco_analysis.RData"
load(rdata)
stopifnot(exists("alldat"), exists("alldat.rfy"), exists("alldat_full"),
          exists("funguild_otu"))                 # funguild_otu <- 8_functional_guilds.R
tab_dir <- if (dir.exists("tables")) "tables" else
           "/home/daniel/Ptarmigan/Scripts_server/Supplementary/tables"
out_dir <- "figures"
dir.create(out_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
grDevices::pdf(NULL)                                 # headless: no X11 fallback

# ---- shared style ----------------------------------------------------------
# Season and guild palettes are the repo standard (8_functional_guilds.R), so one
# colour means one thing across Fig. 1, Fig. 2 and Fig. 4.
season_cols  <- c(Winter = "#0072B2", Summer = "#D55E00")
guild_cols   <- c("Dung saprotroph" = "#E69F00", "Plant-associated" = "#009E73",
                  "Pathotroph" = "#CC79A7", "Other assigned" = "#56B4E9",
                  "Unassigned / dark" = "#999999")
GUILD_LEVELS <- names(guild_cols)

# The one facet vocabulary shared by panels A and B. A carries the strips; B
# repeats the columns beneath it and blanks them, exactly as Fig. 1B does.
Q_LEVELS <- c("q = 0  (richness)", "q = 1  (Shannon)", "q = 2  (Simpson)")

base_theme <- theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold"),
        plot.tag         = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
        plot.subtitle    = element_text(size = 9, colour = "grey30"),
        panel.spacing    = unit(0.8, "lines"),
        legend.key.size  = unit(0.42, "cm"),
        legend.title     = element_text(size = 10),
        legend.text      = element_text(size = 9))

# All in-plot text is ASCII. save_fig() falls back to grDevices::pdf when cairo
# is unavailable, and that device silently substitutes a dot for a Unicode minus
# or delta -- a corrupted PDF that would not fail the build.
pfmt <- function(p) ifelse(is.na(p), "p = NA",
                    ifelse(p < 0.001, "p < 0.001", sprintf("p = %.3f", p)))
to_season <- function(x) factor(c(winter = "Winter", summer = "Summer")[as.character(x)],
                                levels = c("Winter", "Summer"))

# ============================================================================
# Panel A -- season-pool diversity (Section 5.1, Table S8)
# ============================================================================
# Read, never recomputed: 50 rarefaction draws x 100 bootstraps are expensive
# and the estimates are already committed. Pooling samples within a Season asks
# about the Season's whole species pool. These are the DEPTH-CONTROLLED,
# coverage-standardised estimates of Table S8 (every sample rarefied to 12,615
# reads, common coverage), not asymptotic ones: asymptotic richness extrapolates
# to ~2x observed here, and raw incidence carries summer's ~2.6x depth advantage.
asy <- read.csv(file.path(tab_dir, "H2_iNEXT3D_TD_coverage_rarefied.csv"), check.names = FALSE)
stopifnot(setequal(asy$Season, c("Summer", "Winter")), setequal(asy$Order.q, 0:2))
asy$q      <- factor(Q_LEVELS[asy$Order.q + 1], levels = Q_LEVELS)
asy$Season <- factor(asy$Season, levels = c("Winter", "Summer"))
asy$TD_asy <- asy$qTD                                 # plotted estimate (name kept for the ggplot below)
sc_level   <- unique(asy$SC); stopifnot(length(sc_level) == 1L)

pick  <- function(sea) { d <- asy[asy$Season == sea, ]
                         d[match(Q_LEVELS, as.character(d$q)), ] }
A_sum <- pick("Summer"); A_win <- pick("Winter")
# The panel's whole claim in one line: summer above winter at every order, with
# 95% CIs that do not overlap. If that ever stops being true, the build stops.
stopifnot(all(A_sum$qTD.LCL > A_win$qTD.UCL))

pA <- ggplot(asy, aes(Season, TD_asy)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = 1), colour = "grey55", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = qTD.LCL, ymax = qTD.UCL, colour = Season),
                width = 0.12, linewidth = 0.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(aes(fill = Season), shape = 21, size = 3.4,
             colour = "grey25", stroke = 0.4, show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ q, nrow = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = season_cols) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = season_cols) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.18, 0.18))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Season pool\n(effective no. of OTUs)",
       subtitle = sprintf("Pooled-season diversity at equal depth (12,615 reads/sample) and equal coverage (%.2f); iNEXT3D, incidence,\nmedian over 50 rarefaction draws; bars are 95%% CIs. Summer exceeds winter at every order.", sc_level)) +
  base_theme +
  # A's x axis is identical to B's directly below, so only B prints it.
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank()) +
  guides(fill = "none", colour = "none")

# ============================================================================
# Panel B -- per-sample diversity (Section 5.2, Fig. S9 + Table S9)
# ============================================================================
# Raw counts: iNEXT.3D size-standardises internally to rfy_depth, the same depth
# alldat.rfy is rarefied to. Deterministic (an analytic expectation, not one
# rarefaction draw), so no seed is involved; the guard makes that testable.
ps_rfy <- alldat$nopool
m_rfy  <- as(otu_table(ps_rfy), "matrix")
if (taxa_are_rows(ps_rfy)) m_rfy <- t(m_rfy)         # sites x species
rfy_depth <- min(rowSums(m_rfy))
stopifnot(nsamples(ps_rfy) == 52L,
          rfy_depth == unique(rowSums(otu_mat_of(alldat.rfy$nopool))))

md_rfy <- data.frame(as(sample_data(ps_rfy), "data.frame"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
stopifnot(identical(rownames(m_rfy), rownames(md_rfy)))
season_rfy <- to_season(md_rfy$Season); stopifnot(!anyNA(season_rfy))

hill_raw <- hill_inext_size(ps_rfy, level = rfy_depth, label = "Figure 4B")
stopifnot(identical(hill_raw$row, rownames(m_rfy)))
hill <- data.frame(Season = season_rfy,
                   q0 = hill_raw$q0, q1 = hill_raw$q1, q2 = hill_raw$q2)
hill_long <- data.frame(
  Season = rep(hill$Season, times = 3),
  q      = factor(rep(Q_LEVELS, each = nrow(hill)), levels = Q_LEVELS),
  value  = c(hill$q0, hill$q1, hill$q2))

# The annotated contrast is Table S9: a gamma GLM (log link, q ~ Season + Year)
# fitted to exactly the per-sample values plotted here (n = 52), so the figure
# and its test are on the same unit. Guards: the CSV's season means must equal
# the recomputed ones, and the model ratio must agree in direction with them.
lmm <- read.csv(file.path(tab_dir, "H2_season_effect_per_sample.csv"), check.names = FALSE)
stopifnot(setequal(lmm$metric, c("q0", "q1", "q2")), all(lmm$n == nrow(hill)))
lmm <- lmm[match(c("q0", "q1", "q2"), lmm$metric), ]
obs_diff <- vapply(c("q0", "q1", "q2"), function(q)
  mean(hill[[q]][hill$Season == "Summer"]) - mean(hill[[q]][hill$Season == "Winter"]),
  numeric(1))
stopifnot(max(abs(lmm$mean_summer - lmm$mean_winter - obs_diff)) < 1e-8,
          all(sign(obs_diff) == sign(log(lmm$ratio_summer_winter))))

# Boxes show medians, but Section 5.3's text quotes MEANS -- so the means are
# drawn, and the segment joining them is what makes the slope flip legible
# against panel A directly above.
meanB <- aggregate(value ~ q + Season, hill_long, mean)
y_top <- as.numeric(tapply(hill_long$value, hill_long$q, max)[Q_LEVELS])
ann_B <- data.frame(q     = factor(Q_LEVELS, levels = Q_LEVELS),
                    value = y_top * 1.32,
                    lab   = sprintf("summer / winter\n%.2fx, %s",
                                    lmm$ratio_summer_winter, pfmt(lmm$p_season)))

# seed = on the jitter: save_fig() prints the object once per device, and an
# unseeded jitter would place the points differently in the PNG, the JPG and the
# PDF -- three subtly different figures from one build.
pB <- ggplot(hill_long, aes(Season, value)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = Season), outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.6, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.14, height = 0, seed = 1),
             size = 1.1, alpha = 0.55, colour = "grey20") +
  geom_line(data = meanB, aes(group = 1), colour = "grey35", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(data = meanB, shape = 23, size = 2.4, stroke = 0.5,
             fill = "white", colour = "grey15") +
  geom_text(data = ann_B, aes(x = 1.5, label = lab), inherit.aes = TRUE,
            size = 2.9, lineheight = 0.95, vjust = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ q, nrow = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = season_cols) +
  # Linear, not log: a Hill number is an effective number of OTUs and is meant to
  # be read off the axis. free_y absorbs the 164-vs-32 range difference instead.
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.04, 0.36))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Per sample\n(effective no. of OTUs)",
       subtitle = sprintf("Per-sample Hill numbers (n = %d, iNEXT3D size-standardised to %s reads); white diamonds are season means.\nAnnotations: year-adjusted summer/winter ratio, gamma GLM on these values (Table S9).",
                          nrow(hill), format(rfy_depth, big.mark = ","))) +
  base_theme +
  # B repeats A's facet columns exactly, so its strips are dropped as redundant.
  theme(strip.text = element_blank()) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(order = 1))

# ============================================================================
# Panel C -- dominance and evenness, the mechanism (Section 5.3, Table S10)
# ============================================================================
ps  <- alldat$nopool                                 # canonical, raw counts
m   <- as(otu_table(ps), "matrix")
if (!taxa_are_rows(ps)) m <- t(m)                    # taxa x samples, as 5.3 uses
rel <- sweep(m, 2, colSums(m), "/")
stopifnot(all(abs(colSums(rel) - 1) < 1e-10))
md  <- data.frame(as(sample_data(ps), "data.frame"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
stopifnot(identical(colnames(rel), rownames(md)),
          setequal(colnames(rel), rownames(m_rfy)))  # B and C/D are the same 52 birds
season_c <- to_season(md$Season)

pielou_J <- function(p) { p <- p[p > 0]; -sum(p * log(p)) / log(length(p)) }
dom <- data.frame(Season    = season_c,
                  top1_prop = apply(rel, 2, max),
                  pielou_J  = apply(rel, 2, pielou_J))

# Drift guard: the recomputed means must reproduce committed Table S10 exactly at
# the precision the CSV stores (1 dp for the percentage, 2 dp for J).
dom_csv <- read.csv(file.path(tab_dir, "report_dominance_summary.csv"), check.names = FALSE)
dom_csv <- dom_csv[match(c("winter", "summer"), dom_csv$Season), ]
obs_top1 <- tapply(dom$top1_prop, dom$Season, mean)
obs_J    <- tapply(dom$pielou_J,  dom$Season, mean)
stopifnot(max(abs(round(100 * as.numeric(obs_top1[c("Winter","Summer")]), 1) -
                  dom_csv$mean_top1_prop_pct)) < 1e-8,
          max(abs(round(as.numeric(obs_J[c("Winter","Summer")]), 2) -
                  dom_csv$mean_pielou_J)) < 1e-8)
p_top1 <- unique(dom_csv$wilcox_p_top1_prop); p_J <- unique(dom_csv$wilcox_p_pielou_J)
stopifnot(length(p_top1) == 1L, length(p_J) == 1L)

# Both metrics live on 0-1, so one shared axis works and the mechanism reads as a
# single picture: the seasons swap sides between the two metric groups.
# <br> not \n: these labels are rendered by element_markdown, which honours HTML
# breaks. Wrapped because the two names collide at this panel's width.
M_LEVELS <- c("Top-1 OTU<br>read share", "Pielou<br>evenness *J*")
dom_long <- data.frame(
  Season = rep(dom$Season, times = 2),
  Metric = factor(rep(M_LEVELS, each = nrow(dom)), levels = M_LEVELS),
  value  = c(dom$top1_prop, dom$pielou_J))
meanC <- aggregate(value ~ Metric + Season, dom_long, mean)
brk   <- data.frame(Metric = factor(M_LEVELS, levels = M_LEVELS),
                    lab    = pfmt(c(p_top1, p_J)),
                    xmid   = seq_along(M_LEVELS))
brk$xmin <- brk$xmid - 0.19; brk$xmax <- brk$xmid + 0.19  # dodge(0.75) box centres

pC <- ggplot(dom_long, aes(Metric, value, fill = Season)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.65, alpha = 0.85,
               position = position_dodge(width = 0.75)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.12, dodge.width = 0.75,
                                             seed = 1),
             size = 1.1, alpha = 0.55, colour = "grey20", show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(data = meanC, aes(group = Season), inherit.aes = TRUE,
             position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), shape = 23, size = 2.3,
             stroke = 0.5, fill = "white", colour = "grey15", show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_segment(data = brk, aes(x = xmin, xend = xmax, y = 1.03, yend = 1.03),
               inherit.aes = FALSE, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_text(data = brk, aes(x = xmid, y = 1.055, label = lab), inherit.aes = FALSE,
            size = 3, vjust = 0) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = season_cols) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1.13), breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Per-sample value (proportion)",
       subtitle = "White diamonds are season means;\nbrackets give the Wilcoxon rank-sum test (Table S10).") +
  base_theme +
  # The x labels carry markdown (*J*); without element_markdown the asterisks
  # print literally, and this theme() must come after base_theme to win.
  theme(axis.text.x = ggtext::element_markdown(size = 9)) +
  guides(fill = "none")

# ============================================================================
# Panel D -- who the dominants are (Section 5.4, Table S11), by guild
# ============================================================================
top5 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(levels(season_c), function(s) {
  cols   <- colnames(rel)[season_c == s]
  shares <- rowMeans(rel[, cols, drop = FALSE])      # mean WITHIN-season share
  ids    <- names(sort(shares, decreasing = TRUE))[1:5]
  data.frame(Season = s, OTU = ids, share = 100 * shares[ids],
             n_detect = rowSums(rel[ids, cols, drop = FALSE] > 0),
             n_season = length(cols), stringsAsFactors = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
}))
top5$Season <- factor(top5$Season, levels = c("Winter", "Summer"))

# Drift guard: same OTUs, same order, same shares as committed Table S11.
t5_csv <- read.csv(file.path(tab_dir, "report_top5_otu_by_season.csv"),
                   stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
t5_csv$Season <- to_season(t5_csv$Season)
t5_csv <- t5_csv[order(t5_csv$Season, -t5_csv$mean_pct_share), ]
chk    <- top5[order(top5$Season, -top5$share), ]
stopifnot(identical(paste(chk$Season, chk$OTU), paste(t5_csv$Season, t5_csv$OTU)),
          max(abs(round(chk$share, 2) - t5_csv$mean_pct_share)) < 1e-8)

# UNITE taxonomy carries rank prefixes ("g__Thelebolus") and, at species level, a
# trailing hypothesis index ("intermedia 1"). Labels fall back down the ranks
# until something is assigned: a family name stands alone unambiguously, an order
# or class does not and is prefixed "unclassified". Markdown asterisks italicise
# real Latin names only -- never a rank name, never an Incertae sedis placeholder.
tax <- data.frame(as(tax_table(ps), "matrix"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
strip_rank <- function(x) sub("^[a-z]__", "", x)
clean_rank <- function(x) { x <- strip_rank(x)
  x[is.na(x) | x == "" | x == "NA" | grepl("unidentified", x, ignore.case = TRUE)] <- NA_character_
  x }
otu_label <- function(otu) {
  rk <- lapply(c("Genus", "Species", "Family", "Order", "Class"),
               function(r) clean_rank(tax[otu, r]))
  names(rk) <- c("Genus", "Species", "Family", "Order", "Class")
  incertae <- function(x) !is.na(x) && grepl("Incertae_sedis", x)
  nm <-
    if (!is.na(rk$Genus) && !incertae(rk$Genus)) {
      if (!is.na(rk$Species))
        paste0("*", rk$Genus, " ", sub("[ _]+[0-9]+$", "", rk$Species), "*")
      else paste0("*", rk$Genus, "*")
    } else if (incertae(rk$Genus))                      sub("_gen_Incertae_sedis", " (unclass.)", rk$Genus)
      else if (!is.na(rk$Family) && !incertae(rk$Family)) rk$Family
      else if (!is.na(rk$Order))                        paste("unclassified", rk$Order)
      else if (!is.na(rk$Class))                        paste("unclassified", rk$Class)
      else                                              "unclassified fungus"
  paste0(nm, " (", otu, ")")
}
top5$label <- unname(vapply(top5$OTU, otu_label, character(1)))
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(top5$label))

# Guild rule VERBATIM from the Fig. 1 chunk (itself from 8_functional_guilds.R),
# including its genus cleaning, so Fig. 1, Fig. 4, Section 8 and Section 9 all
# classify an OTU identically. One consequence is visible here: FUNGuild returns
# a compound string for Candida parapsilosis containing "Epiphyte", so the
# priority rule lands OTU136 in Plant-associated. That is an artifact of compound
# FUNGuild strings, not a claim about the taxon -- but the rule is applied
# unchanged rather than special-cased, because cross-section consistency is worth
# more than one prettier label.
COPRO_GENERA <- c("Sordaria","Podospora","Cercophora","Chaetomium","Schizothecium",
                  "Preussia","Delitschia","Pilobolus","Ascobolus","Saccobolus",
                  "Sporormiella","Coprinopsis","Thelebolus","Coniochaeta")
gen       <- strip_rank(tax$Genus[match(top5$OTU, rownames(tax))])
gen       <- ifelse(gen %in% c("", "NA"), NA, gen)
guild_str <- funguild_otu$Guild[match(top5$OTU, funguild_otu$OTU_ID)]
is_copro  <- (!is.na(guild_str) & grepl("Dung Saprotroph", guild_str)) |
             (!is.na(gen)       & gen %in% COPRO_GENERA)
is_plant  <- !is_copro & !is.na(guild_str) &
             grepl("Endophyte|Plant Saprotroph|Plant Pathogen|Epiphyte", guild_str)
is_patho  <- !is_copro & !is_plant & !is.na(guild_str) & grepl("Pathogen|Parasite", guild_str)
top5$Guild <- factor(
  ifelse(is_copro, "Dung saprotroph",
  ifelse(is_plant, "Plant-associated",
  ifelse(is_patho, "Pathotroph",
  ifelse(!is.na(guild_str), "Other assigned", "Unassigned / dark")))),
  levels = GUILD_LEVELS)

# The two seasons' top-5 sets are disjoint, so one global factor ordered
# (Season, share) gives each facet its own descending bars under free_y.
top5 <- top5[order(top5$Season, top5$share), ]
top5$label <- factor(top5$label, levels = top5$label)
n_lab <- setNames(sprintf("%s (n = %d)", levels(season_c), as.integer(table(season_c))),
                  levels(season_c))

pD <- ggplot(top5, aes(share, label, fill = Guild)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72, colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f%%  (%d/%d)", share, n_detect, n_season)),
            hjust = -0.12, size = 2.8, colour = "grey25") +
  facet_grid(Season ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y",
             labeller = labeller(Season = n_lab)) +
  # drop = TRUE: "Other assigned" has no member among these ten OTUs and a key
  # with no bar is noise; the level ORDER stays the repo-canonical one.
  scale_fill_manual(values = guild_cols, name = "Functional guild", drop = TRUE) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.32))) +
  labs(x = "Mean within-season read share (%)", y = NULL,
       subtitle = "Bar labels give the mean share and, in parentheses,\nthe number of that season's samples with any detection.") +
  base_theme +
  theme(axis.text.y = ggtext::element_markdown(size = 9)) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(order = 2, nrow = 2))

# ---- assemble and write ----------------------------------------------------
# An explicit design grid, not nested `/` and `|`: patchwork FLATTENS a chain of
# `/`, so (pA / pB) / (pC | pD) silently becomes a three-row layout and errors.
# The grid also guarantees what panel A and B depend on -- one shared column
# geometry, so their facet columns line up and the slope flip reads vertically.
# D gets five of the eight columns because its taxon labels are up to 38 chars.
design <- "
AAAAAAAA
BBBBBBBB
CCCDDDDD
"
fig4 <- pA + pB + pC + pD +
  plot_layout(design = design, heights = c(1, 1.18, 1.55), guides = "collect") +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.box = "horizontal")

# Written as PNG (600 dpi) and PDF (vector).
save_fig <- function(stem, obj, width, height, res = 600) {
  one <- function(open_dev) { open_dev(); on.exit(grDevices::dev.off()); print(obj) }
  one(function() grDevices::png(paste0(stem, ".png"), width = width, height = height,
                                units = "in", res = res))
  pdf_dev <- if (capabilities("cairo")) grDevices::cairo_pdf else grDevices::pdf
  one(function() pdf_dev(paste0(stem, ".pdf"), width = width, height = height))
}
save_fig(file.path(out_dir, "S8b_richness_evenness_crossover"), fig4, 10, 10.4)

# ---- console summary -------------------------------------------------------
cat("Season-pool diversity, depth-controlled and coverage-standardised (Table S8):\n")
print(data.frame(q = Q_LEVELS,
                 summer = sprintf("%.0f [%.0f, %.0f]", A_sum$TD_asy, A_sum$qTD.LCL, A_sum$qTD.UCL),
                 winter = sprintf("%.0f [%.0f, %.0f]", A_win$TD_asy, A_win$qTD.LCL, A_win$qTD.UCL)),
      row.names = FALSE)
hill_means <- aggregate(cbind(q0, q1, q2) ~ Season, hill, mean)
hill_means[-1] <- round(hill_means[-1], 2)
cat(sprintf("\nPer-sample Hill means (n = %d, size-standardised to %d reads):\n", nrow(hill), rfy_depth))
print(hill_means, row.names = FALSE)
cat("\nPer-sample gamma GLM, summer/winter ratio (n = 52; Table S9):\n")
print(data.frame(metric = lmm$metric, ratio = round(lmm$ratio_summer_winter, 3),
                 lwr = round(lmm$ratio_lwr, 3), upr = round(lmm$ratio_upr, 3),
                 p = signif(lmm$p_season, 3)), row.names = FALSE)
cat(sprintf("\nTop-1 OTU read share: summer %.1f%% vs winter %.1f%%  (%s)\n",
            100 * obs_top1[["Summer"]], 100 * obs_top1[["Winter"]], pfmt(p_top1)))
cat(sprintf("Pielou evenness J   : summer %.2f  vs winter %.2f   (%s)\n",
            obs_J[["Summer"]], obs_J[["Winter"]], pfmt(p_J)))
cat("\nTop-5 OTUs per season (mean within-season read share):\n")
print(data.frame(Season = chk$Season, OTU = chk$OTU, share_pct = round(chk$share, 2),
                 detected = sprintf("%d/%d", chk$n_detect, chk$n_season),
                 guild = as.character(top5$Guild[match(chk$OTU, top5$OTU)])),
      row.names = FALSE)
```

#### Documentation notes — Section 5 {.unnumbered}

This dark, winter-associated OTU is an **E1** dark taxon (Section 3.4) — and, being winter-persistent, a candidate to carry into the deferred H3 plant-covariation analysis downstream — and it revises the original "stable cold-adapted *Thelebolus*–*Sporormiella* core" framing: those recognizable coprophilous genera are part of the summer-inflated, activity-tracking tail, not a season-independent core.
:::

## Section 6: Lineage-specific seasonal responses — GLLVM (H1, OTU-resolved) {.page-break-before}

Sections 4 and 5 establish that the community shifts between seasons (H1) and that summer samples gain a long rare tail while becoming more dominance-skewed (H2). This section resolves H1 to the level of individual OTUs. We fit a generalized linear latent-variable model (GLLVM, negative-binomial) of per-OTU counts as a function of Season (winter as reference), with a library-size offset and random intercepts for individual bird and PCR replicate; the model is fitted on the full-complexity, one-row-per-PCR-replicate object (`Scripts/7_gllvm.R`, objects `models/fit_nb_2.rds` and `models/fit_nb_2_2.rds`). It answers which lineages drive the turnover — each with its own model uncertainty — and, through its latent variables, describes the residual co-occurrence that remains after Season is accounted for.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
<!-- SEE NOTE: a real scientific limitation, not a status note — you may want one plain sentence of this to survive into the submitted version -->

::: callout-warning
**Fitted on the pre-depth-fix object.** These fits were built on the full-complexity object as it stood *before* the July depth-filter correction: 57 samples (114 PCR-replicate rows) and 327 filtered OTUs, versus the 52-sample / 278-OTU canonical object used everywhere else in this appendix. The library-size offset, per-OTU abundance weights, and the Poisson baseline in Table S-GLLVMa are all reconstructed from that same pre-fix object so the section is internally consistent. The five extra samples and larger OTU set do not change the direction or rank of any result below, but exact coefficients will move slightly when the models are refitted on the corrected object — treat the numbers as robust in sign and rank, provisional in the last digit.
:::
:::

::: callout-warning
**Read the per-OTU coefficients in this section as signs and ranks, not effect sizes.** Two limitations apply. (i) The models were fitted on the pre-depth-filter-correction object (57 samples, 114 replicate rows, 327 OTUs), not the canonical 52-sample object used elsewhere. (ii) Many Season coefficients are not estimable as finite effects: OTUs absent or nearly absent from one season push an unpooled fixed coefficient toward ±∞. 134 of the 327 OTUs are flagged for this (`separation`), and 101 of the 209 OTUs counted as significant are among them (the largest reaching β ≈ 1,295 on the log scale). Among the 193 unflagged OTUs, 106 still have \|β\| \> 10, i.e. implausible fold changes (e¹⁰ ≈ 22,000), including the *Sporormiella* and *Coniochaeta* values quoted below (β ≈ 17). The OTU-level seasonal pattern is carried by HMSC in Section 9, which is fitted on the current data with shrinkage.
:::

### 6.1 Model choice

```{r tab-gllvm-aic}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
mc <- read.csv("tables/gllvm_model_comparison.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
mc$logLik <- signif(mc$logLik, 4); mc$AIC <- signif(mc$AIC, 5); mc$dAIC <- signif(mc$dAIC, 4)
kable(mc[, c("model", "logLik", "AIC", "dAIC")],
      col.names = c("Model", "logLik", "AIC", "ΔAIC"),
      caption = "Table S-GLLVMa. GLLVM model comparison on the same 327-OTU / 114-row response matrix. The negative-binomial fits are dramatically better than the Poisson baseline (strong overdispersion), and two latent variables are preferred over one (ΔAIC ≈ 723). fit_nb_2_2 is the reported model.")
```

The negative-binomial family is strongly favoured over Poisson (the Poisson log-likelihood is worse by \~5 orders of magnitude, the signature of severe count overdispersion), and two latent variables outperform one by ΔAIC ≈ 723. We therefore report `fit_nb_2_2` (negative-binomial, two latent variables).

### 6.2 Which OTUs drive the seasonal turnover

For every OTU we extract the Season coefficient (β on the GLLVM log scale; positive = higher in summer) together with the model's own Wald 95% CI, and flag significance at a Benjamini–Hochberg FDR of 5%.

![](figures/gllvm_perOTU_season_coef.png)

**Figure S-GLLVMa**: Season response of the 30 most abundant OTUs, each with its model 95% CI, coloured by Order; filled points are significant at BH q \< 0.05. Of the 327 modelled OTUs, 209 are significant, and the turnover is strongly asymmetric: 166 OTUs are enriched in summer versus 43 in winter. A further 134 OTUs are near-complete "on/off" seasonal switches (essentially absent in one season); these have real but non-interpretable point estimates (β in the hundreds, or exploding CIs) and are flagged (`separation`) and excluded both from this panel and from Table S-GLLVMb, which reports only well-estimated OTUs; they are retained in the full per-OTU table (`tables/gllvm_perOTU_season_coef.csv`).

```{r tab-gllvm-otu}
#| echo: false
suppressMessages(library(dplyr)); library(knitr)
oc  <- read.csv("tables/gllvm_perOTU_season_coef.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
well <- oc %>% filter(!separation, sig)
fmt <- function(df) df %>% transmute(OTU = taxon, Genus, Order,
                                     beta = round(beta_season, 2),
                                     `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.1f, %.1f]", ci_lo, ci_hi),
                                     `BH q` = signif(p_adj, 2))
kable(well %>% arrange(desc(beta_season)) %>% slice_head(n = 8) %>% fmt(),
      caption = "Table S-GLLVMb(i). Most strongly summer-enriched well-estimated OTUs (BH q < 0.05).")
kable(well %>% arrange(beta_season) %>% slice_head(n = 8) %>% fmt(),
      caption = "Table S-GLLVMb(ii). Most strongly winter-enriched well-estimated OTUs (BH q < 0.05). Full per-OTU table: tables/gllvm_perOTU_season_coef.csv.")
```

Two results connect directly to the dominance analysis (Section 5.4). The coprophilous taxa that dominate summer read share behave differently under the model: OTU636 (*Sporormiella*, β ≈ 17.2) and OTU1225 (*Coniochaeta*, β ≈ 17.3) are both significantly summer-enriched, but OTU1 (*Thelebolus*, β ≈ 3.0) is not significant (95% CI crosses zero) — its large summer read share is carried by a few samples and high among-individual variance rather than a model-robust per-OTU shift. On the winter side, the dark taxon OTU1369 (class Dothideomycetes) is significantly winter-enriched (β ≈ −6.9): the GLLVM independently corroborates the dominance/E1 finding that winter's persistent OTU is a taxonomically unresolved lineage.

Aggregating to genus gives the broader pattern:

![](figures/panel_AB_heatmap_barplot_season.png)

**Figure S-GLLVMc**: Genus-level seasonal response. (A) Heatmap of the abundance-weighted mean β per genus; (B) the same as a point-range plot with bootstrapped 95% CIs. Warm = summer-enriched, cool = winter-enriched.

```{r tab-gllvm-genus}
#| echo: false
suppressMessages(library(dplyr)); library(knitr)
gt <- read.csv("tables/genus_table_season.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
gt %>% transmute(Order, Genus, n_OTUs,
                 `total reads` = round(total_w_abund),
                 `median beta` = round(median_beta_season, 1),
                 `weighted-mean beta` = round(w_mean_beta_season, 1)) %>%
  arrange(desc(`weighted-mean beta`)) %>%
  kable(caption = "Table S-GLLVMc. Genus-level seasonal responses (β = summer vs winter, GLLVM log scale) for genera passing the abundance/effect-size thresholds. Full detail in models/genus_table_season.csv.")
```

### 6.3 Residual co-occurrence beyond Season

![](figures/gllvm_residual_ordination.png)

**Figure S-GLLVMb**: Model-based ordination on the two latent variables of `fit_nb_2_2` — the residual OTU co-occurrence structure that remains *after* Season and the random effects are accounted for. Sites are coloured by Season; the eight strongest species loadings are labelled. This is the model-based counterpart to the unconstrained robust-Aitchison PCoA in Section 4.1: because Season is already in the model as a fixed effect, the two seasons overlap substantially here, confirming that Season captures a coherent axis of the community rather than all of its covariation. A small set of winter sites separates along the second latent variable (winter scores are \~3.4× as variable as summer ones on that axis, Fligner–Killeen p = 0.013; seven of the eight most extreme sites are winter). This is specific to that axis and is not a statement about which season is more heterogeneous overall — on the first latent variable summer is the more variable season, and Section 4.2 finds summer significantly the more dispersed in total composition (mean distance to centroid 24.8 versus 13.6, p = 0.002).

## Section 7: Diet-tracking and Bayesian models — H2 and H3 {.page-break-before}

### 7.1 Diet richness and fungal diversity — Bayesian mechanism (H2)

Section 5 tested the seasonal part of H2. Here we test its mechanism directly, on the samples that have paired plant ITS2 diet data and pass the 10,000-read depth filter of Sections 4–5 (**n = 27** dung samples): does an individual sample's fungal diversity track the richness of its own dietary plant community? Fungal Hill diversity is modelled as a function of standardised plant (diet) richness, adjusting for Season, in a Bayesian Gamma regression with a log link (brms). H2's mechanism is supported if the plant-richness slope is positive with posterior probability P(slope \> 0) \> 0.95. Three further diet-matched winter samples (2,975–7,167 reads) are excluded here because the outcome is a per-sample diversity estimate standardised to a common depth of 12,615 reads (Section 5), and including them would force that depth down for every sample; the count models of Sections 7.2–7.3 retain them (n = 30) because they account for depth with a per-library offset instead.

The preregistration specified Year and individual bird as random intercepts. At this matched sample size that structure is unidentifiable — the 27 samples come from 24 distinct birds, so an individual random effect cannot be separated from residual variation, and Year spans only three levels — and the random-effects model does not converge. We therefore report two complementary, cleanly-converged fixed-effect models that bracket the estimate: a **Season-adjusted** model (`plant_richness + Season + Year`, Year as a fixed effect) and a more parsimonious **drop-Year** model (`plant_richness + Season`). Both model the raw Hill number with a Gamma likelihood and log link, the same family as the per-sample Season test of Table S9, with a weakly-informative prior on the slope (Normal(0, 1) per standard deviation of plant richness, on the log scale).

![](figures/H2_diet_richness_fit.png)

**Figure S9**: Per-sample fungal Hill q1 diversity against rarefied dietary plant richness (n = 27 matched samples), coloured by Season. Both Gamma (log link) model fits are shown — Season-adjusted (solid) and drop-Year (dashed) — with the 95% credible ribbon for the primary Season-adjusted model. Fitted lines are drawn at the reference Season/Year; the quantity of interest is the common positive slope.

```{r tab-h2mech-compare}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
mc <- read.csv("tables/H2_mechanism_model_comparison.csv", check.names = FALSE)
mc_disp <- data.frame(
  Model       = mc$model,
  Structure   = mc$formula,
  `Slope (median, log scale)` = round(mc$median, 3),
  `95% CrI`   = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", mc$lwr95, mc$upr95),
  `Ratio per SD` = sprintf("%.2f", exp(mc$median)),
  `P(slope>0)`= round(mc$P_gt0, 3),
  Divergences = mc$divergences,
  `Clears 0.95?` = ifelse(mc$supported, "yes", "no"),
  check.names = FALSE)
kable(mc_disp,
      caption = "Table S12. H2-mechanism: the two complementary Bayesian Gamma (log link) models of fungal Hill q1 diversity vs. dietary plant richness. Slopes are on the log scale per standard deviation of plant richness; 'Ratio per SD' = exp(median slope), the multiplicative change in fungal Hill q1. Both converge cleanly (0 divergences, Rhat < 1.01) and place the diet-richness slope positive.")
```

:::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
```{r tab-h2mech-family}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
fc <- read.csv("tables/H2_mechanism_family_choice.csv", check.names = FALSE)
kable(data.frame(
  Family      = fc$family,
  Model       = fc$model,
  `Slope (median)` = sprintf("%.3f (%s)", fc$median, fc$slope_scale),
  `95% CrI`   = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", fc$lwr95, fc$upr95),
  `P(slope>0)`= round(fc$P_gt0, 3),
  `PPC skewness p` = round(fc$ppc_p_skewness, 3),
  `ΔELPD vs primary (SE)` = sprintf("%.1f (%.1f)", fc$elpd_diff_vs_primary, fc$se_diff),
  check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "Table S12b (documentation build). Family choice for the H2-mechanism model. Until 2026-09 the model was Gaussian on the z-scored Hill number; it fails the posterior-predictive skewness check (Bayesian p ≈ 0) and is outperformed by ≈ 13 ELPD (PSIS-LOO on the raw q1 scale). Gamma and lognormal fit equally well; Gamma was adopted because Table S9 already uses it. Source: 6_diversity_analyses.R Section 3b; pilot comparison of further families in model_development/brms_refit/README.md.")
```
::::

Both models place the diet-richness slope on the positive side (medians +0.22 and +0.34 on the log scale, i.e. fungal Hill q1 multiplied by 1.24 and 1.40 per standard deviation of plant richness), with posterior support of **P(slope \> 0) = 0.91** (Season-adjusted) and **0.99** (drop-Year). The drop-Year model clears the preregistered 0.95 threshold; the Season-adjusted model, whose 95% credible interval includes zero, sits just below it. The direction of the effect is consistent between the two models, but only the drop-Year model meets the preregistered criterion.

![](figures/H2_mechanism_slope_posterior.png)

**Figure S10**: Posterior distribution of the diet-richness slope (log scale, per standard deviation of plant richness) for both Gamma models. The mass of both posteriors lies to the right of zero (dashed line).

The signal is consistent across the choice of Hill order: refitting with richness (q0) and Simpson-equivalent (q2) diversity as the outcome gives positive slopes throughout, with P(slope \> 0) between 0.78 and 0.99 (Table S13). No specification reverses the direction.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
<!-- DANIEL (exp/brms-refit, 2026-10-01): numbers above are updated to the Gamma models; the interpretive
prose below is untouched and yours to rewrite. Two points from the refit bear on it: (1) "primarily at the
seasonal scale" is backwards — Season is in both models, so the slope IS within-season, and the
between-season contrast runs the other way (2026-09-10 Hill-order memo); (2) under every family tried,
removing S_1_7_P1_8E takes P(slope > 0) to ~0.5 (Table S14 most-influential sample). -->

**Ecological interpretation.** Dietary plant richness is markedly higher in summer than winter, so most of the diet–diversity relationship is expressed through the *seasonal* contrast — which is exactly the diet-driven mechanism H2 proposes: the seasonal diet shift is the dominant axis of variation in propagule supply, and summer's richer plant intake is accompanied by a richer fungal community. Within a single season the diet-richness gradient is short (only a few plant OTUs separate one sample from another), so the per-sample effect is correspondingly modest.

Consistent with a modest, gradient-limited signal at this sample size, the estimate is carried by the samples at the extremes of the diet-richness range: a single leave-one-out omission moves the slope within the ranges in Table S14, and rank (Spearman) correlations within each Season are close to zero — the parametric slope reflects the between-season spread of the gradient more than fine within-season covariation. The honest reading is therefore a **weak, directionally-consistent signal**: fungal diversity does tend to rise with dietary plant richness, primarily at the seasonal scale, but the per-sample effect is not resolved decisively at n = 27 and is a clear target for a larger diet-matched sample.
:::

The result is a directionally consistent but unresolved signal: fungal diversity tends to rise with dietary plant richness, but the slope is not resolved at n = 27 and depends largely on a single dropping (Table S14); testing it properly needs a larger diet-matched sample.

Robustness of the diet-richness slope: leave-one-out influence (slope of the equivalent frequentist Gamma GLM on the log scale, its range across single-sample omissions, and the most influential sample) and Spearman rank correlations overall and within each Season. ### 7.2 OTU–plant covariation — Bayesian hurdle model (H3)

Section 7.1 asked whether overall fungal diversity tracks overall diet richness. H3 is finer-grained and taxon-resolved: does each fungal OTU covary with particular diet-plant taxa, and — the preregistered contrast — do recognised coprophilous taxa show the diffuse, non-specific plant associations expected of dung specialists dispersed independently of any host plant, while other taxa may show the tight, single-plant covariation that would flag a likely ingested endophyte passenger? Inference is strictly forward-directional: a tight single-plant association is read as evidence of a likely ingested passenger; a diffuse or absent association is not read as evidence of gut/dung residency.

**Model.** We fit a single hierarchical hurdle negative-binomial model (brms) to the diet-matched subset. To retain as many matched samples as possible we use the PCR-replicate-level, minimally depth-filtered object (mirroring the GLLVM of Section 6) rather than the collapsed, 10,000-read-filtered object of Sections 4–5; this recovers three additional low-depth winter dung samples that carry paired plant data, raising the matched subset to **n = 30 biological samples (60 PCR-replicate libraries; 19 winter, 11 summer)**. Forty-six OTUs present in ≥5 of the 30 samples are modelled. The hurdle model has two parts: whether an OTU is detected in a library (**occurrence**) and how abundant it is when detected (**abundance given presence**). Both parts carry Season, Year and four diet-plant predictors, each with a community-wide coefficient and a per-OTU deviation (partial pooling); the abundance part also has a per-replicate log-library-size offset and a per-OTU biological-sample random effect, so the two PCR replicates of a sample are treated as replication rather than independent samples. The preregistered "individual" random effect is replaced by the sample effect for the same reason as in Section 7.1. The diet predictors are the four plant taxa present as ≥1% of diet reads in at least seven matched samples — *Betula* (resolved only to genus), *Vaccinium myrtillus*, *V. uliginosum* and *Empetrum nigrum* — each as a centred log-ratio of its share of the diet (zero reads set to 0.1% of the diet), standardised. Occurrence slopes are reported on the detection scale: positive means the OTU is detected more often as that plant rises in the diet. Because a slope shared by every OTU is not specificity, an OTU–plant association counts as **resolved** when the OTU's own deviation from the community-wide slope has a 95% credible interval excluding zero. Per-OTU specificity is summarised, separately for each part, by a Herfindahl–Hirschman index (HHI) of the \|plant slopes\| (0.25 if spread evenly across the four plants, 1 if concentrated on one), and the preregistered contrast compares it between FUNGuild-flagged coprophilous OTUs and plant-associated (endophyte/phyllosphere/plant-saprotroph) OTUs. The model converged cleanly (no divergent transitions, maximum R̂ = 1.004, minimum bulk ESS 1,034) and reproduces the observed mean count and the per-OTU fraction of zeros (r = 0.99 between observed and predicted); its negative-binomial tail predicts occasional counts above the largest library size.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
**What changed (2026-10-01, branch `exp/brms-refit`).** Until 2026-09 this section used a joint negative-binomial model with six plant genera transformed by `decostand("rclr")`, a single community-wide Season coefficient and one overdispersion parameter. Three problems surfaced: the rCLR imputes zeros by rank-3 matrix completion, so the six predictors were exactly rank 3 and half of each OTU's plant slopes were set by the prior; per-OTU seasonality leaked into the plant slopes (*Vaccinium* is the summer diet at this site, *Betula* the winter one); and the single negative-binomial shape (0.024) predicted mean counts about five times too high. A pilot of nine likelihood × structure variants found the hurdle model to be the only one that converged and reproduced the data (`model_development/brms_refit/README.md`). The old model's single resolved association (*Thelebolus*–*Vaccinium*) does not survive the correction.
:::

![](figures/H3_perOTU_plant_coef.png)

**Figure S11**: Each modelled fungal OTU's slope on each diet plant (posterior median of the community slope plus the OTU's deviation), for abundance given presence (left; log scale) and occurrence (right; log-odds of detection). Rows are grouped by FUNGuild guild class; red = higher with more of that plant in the diet, blue = lower. Dots mark the ten OTU–plant deviations whose 95% credible interval excludes zero — all in the occurrence part.

:::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
**Result.** No OTU differs resolvably from the others in how its abundance (given presence) tracks any diet plant: all 184 abundance-part deviations have credible intervals spanning zero, and the spread of OTU deviations is small for every plant (Table S15b). The plant signal lies in occurrence. There, OTUs differ most in their association with *Betula* (SD of OTU deviations 0.91) and *Empetrum nigrum* (0.46), and least with the two *Vaccinium* species (0.25 and 0.13). Ten occurrence associations are resolved (Table S15). Eight involve *Betula*: the coprophilous OTU636 (*Sporormiella*), OTU1225 (*Coniochaeta*) and OTU1305, the plant-associated OTU758 (*Meristemomyces*), OTU483 and OTU554 (*Exobasidium*), and OTU97 are detected less often the more *Betula* dominates the diet, while the dark Dothideomycete OTU1369 is detected more often. Two involve *Empetrum*: OTU45 (*Coleophoma*, plant-associated) and OTU2 (Myriangiales) are detected more often when *Empetrum* is in the diet. At the community level, a higher share of *V. myrtillus* in the diet goes with fewer OTUs being detected (−0.58 \[−0.89, −0.29\]), and *Empetrum* with more (+0.32 \[0.11, 0.53\]). The preregistered contrast is not supported in either part: the coprophilous group is not more diffuse than the plant-associated group (abundance: median HHI 0.35 vs 0.36, one-sided Wilcoxon p = 0.45, P(coprophilous more diffuse) = 0.48; occurrence: 0.35 vs 0.33, p = 0.72, P = 0.37; Table S16). Fitting the same model with the three plant genera instead of four species gives the same *Betula* and *Empetrum* slopes (r = 0.98–0.996 across OTUs) and the same two *Empetrum* associations.
::::

**Result.** All 184 abundance-part deviations have credible intervals spanning zero; the ten resolved associations are all in the occurrence part (Table S15). There, OTUs differ most in their association with *Betula* (SD of OTU deviations 0.91) and *Empetrum nigrum* (0.46), and least with the two *Vaccinium* species (0.25 and 0.13). At the community level, a higher share of *V. myrtillus* in the diet goes with fewer OTUs being detected (−0.58 \[−0.89, −0.29\]) and *Empetrum* with more (+0.32 \[0.11, 0.53\]) (Table S15b). The preregistered contrast is null in both parts (abundance: median HHI 0.35 vs 0.36, one-sided Wilcoxon p = 0.45, P(coprophilous more diffuse) = 0.48; occurrence: 0.35 vs 0.33, p = 0.72, P = 0.37; Table S16). Fitting the same model with the three plant genera instead of four species gives the same *Betula* and *Empetrum* slopes (r = 0.98–0.996 across OTUs) and the same two *Empetrum* associations.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
*Pre-refit interpretation (2026-07 joint negative-binomial model with six rank-3 genus predictors; superseded — kept for reference, its Thelebolus–Vaccinium result no longer holds):*

**Interpretation.** H3, as preregistered, is **not supported**: taxonomically recognised coprophilous taxa do *not* show more diffuse plant associations than other taxa — if anything the reverse. The single interpretable plant signal is a *Vaccinium*–*Thelebolus* covariation, and its ecology is the opposite of the "ingested passenger" reading H3 was built to detect: *Thelebolus* is a dung specialist, and *Vaccinium* (with *Empetrum*) is the winter browse of ptarmigan at this site. Because Season is already a covariate this is a within-season-adjusted association, but the residual gradient is short; the most parsimonious reading is that the winter-browse plants and the persistent dung-fungal core co-vary as parallel seasonal signatures of the same samples, not that *Thelebolus* is carried into the gut on *Vaccinium* tissue. This dovetails with Section 6, where *Thelebolus* (OTU1) was the one coprophile *without* a clean seasonal differential-abundance signal, and with the coprophilous-genus screen in Section 3.2.
:::

**Limitation.** Even at n = 30 the diet is dominated by a few plants (*Betula* near-ubiquitous and near-pure in winter 2023–2024, then *Vaccinium* in summer and *Empetrum*), so specificity can be assessed over only four plant species, winter diet variation comes almost entirely from 2022, and the coprophilous group is small (6 OTUs). We therefore report H3 as a directional, exploratory result rather than a decisive test — and, consistent with the forward-directional inference rule, the absence of tight single-plant passenger signatures is **not** evidence that the dung mycobiome is gut-resident. A larger, more diet-even matched sample is the necessary next step.
