### 7.3 OTU–plant covariation — GLLVM cross-check (H3)

To check that the H3 verdict of Section 7.2 is not an artefact of one modelling framework, we repeat the analysis with a generalised linear latent-variable model (GLLVM) — the same model-based framework used for the OTU-resolved H1 in Section 6, now with the diet-plant predictors added. Everything about the data is held identical to the Bayesian model: the same PCR-replicate-level matched subset (**n = 30 biological samples, 60 libraries; 46 OTUs present in ≥5 samples**), the same four standardised diet-plant predictors (Section 7.2), the same per-library log-size offset, and the same specificity index and preregistered coprophilous-vs-plant-associated contrast. Only the estimator differs.

**Model.** Each OTU's counts are modelled with a negative-binomial GLLVM (`gllvm`), with per-OTU (species-specific) *fixed* coefficients for Season, Year and each diet plant, a biological-sample random row effect (so the two PCR replicates of a sample count as replication, not independent samples), and the log-library-size offset. `gllvm` has no hurdle family, so each slope here mixes occurrence and abundance. We fit 0, 1 and 2 residual latent variables and select by AIC; here **num.lv = 0** is preferred — beyond the sample random effect the latent variables capture no further residual co-occurrence (so, unlike Section 6, there is no residual ordination to show). One difference from the Bayesian model is forced by the software: the natural partial-pooling analog (`gllvm`'s `randomX` species-specific *random* slopes) is silently dropped on this dataset, returning no plant-slope parameters at all. We therefore estimate the plant slopes as *fixed* per-OTU coefficients with Wald standard errors — an **unpooled** frequentist estimate that brackets the Bayesian *pooled* one from the other side. Rare on/off OTUs push their fixed coefficients toward ±∞ (near-separation); as in Section 6 these are flagged (15 of 46 OTUs) and excluded from the specificity ranking, contrast and plots, leaving **31 well-estimated OTUs**. Specificity is the same Herfindahl index of the \|plant slopes\|; a *resolved single-plant association* here means the 90 % Wald interval of an OTU's strongest plant slope excludes zero.

::: callout-warning
**Caveat on the per-OTU slopes.** Even among the 31 retained OTUs the unpooled slopes are very large for a per-SD predictor (median \|slope\| 3.7, 90th percentile 14.0, maximum 28.8 on the log scale), because each OTU carries its own unpooled Season, Year and plant coefficients estimated from 30 samples. The count of Wald-resolved associations in this section therefore overstates what is estimable; the pooled Bayesian model of Section 7.2 resolves 10 OTU-specific associations, all in occurrence. What this section can support is the model-level verdict and the direction of the associations (Table S20b), not the individual slope sizes.
:::

```{r tab-h3g-aic}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
mc <- read.csv("tables/gllvm_H3_model_comparison.csv", check.names = FALSE)
kable(data.frame(
  Model    = mc$model,
  `num.lv` = mc$num_lv,
  Plants   = ifelse(mc$plants, "yes", "no"),
  logLik   = round(mc$logLik, 1),
  AIC      = round(mc$AIC, 1),
  dAIC     = round(mc$dAIC, 1),
  check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "Table S18. GLLVM H3 model comparison (AIC). Latent variables add nothing beyond the sample random effect (num.lv = 0 preferred among the plant models), and the plant model is AIC-preferred over the Season + Year null (dAIC ≈ 220). Because the unpooled plant slopes are very large (see the caveat above), part of that likelihood gain may come from near-separated OTUs; read it as 'diet adds information', not as support for any individual slope.")
```

```{r tab-h3g-agree}
      caption = "Table S20c. The ten OTU–plant associations resolved by the Bayesian model (Table S15, all occurrence) as estimated by the GLLVM.")
```

**Result.** The GLLVM reaches the **same verdict as the Bayesian model on the preregistered contrast — H3 is not supported**: the coprophilous group is not more diffuse than the plant-associated group (median specificity 0.34 vs 0.33, one-sided Wilcoxon p = 0.79, P(coprophilous more diffuse) = 0.39; genus-list grouping 0.33 vs 0.33, p = 0.61; Table S20). Diet does improve the model (AIC prefers the plant model over the Season + Year null by ≈ 220), and the unpooled Wald intervals resolve a single-plant association for 22 of the 31 well-estimated OTUs, with 12 of 124 OTU × plant slopes significant at BH q < 0.05 — numbers inflated by the absence of shrinkage (see caveat). On direction the two frameworks partly agree. GLLVM slopes track the Bayesian *occurrence* slopes for *Betula* (Spearman ρ = 0.49), *Empetrum nigrum* (0.50) and *V. uliginosum* (0.71), but not for *V. myrtillus* (−0.07), and do not track the abundance slopes (Table S20b). Of the ten associations the Bayesian model resolves, the GLLVM gives the same sign for eight and a 95% CI excluding zero for six — *Coleophoma* (OTU45) and OTU2 with *Empetrum*, and *Coniochaeta* (OTU1225), OTU1305, *Sporormiella* (OTU636) and *Exobasidium* (OTU554) lower with *Betula* (Table S20c).

![](figures/gllvm_H3_specificity_contrast.png)

**Figure S14**: Per-OTU GLLVM specificity by FUNGuild guild class (frequentist counterpart of Figure S12). Coprophilous OTUs are not resolvably more diffuse than plant-associated ones. Dashed line = maximally-diffuse baseline (1/4).

```{r tab-h3g-contrast}

ct <- read.csv("tables/gllvm_H3_specificity_contrast.csv", check.names = FALSE)
kable(data.frame(

  `n copro`                   = ct$n_coprophilous,
  `n plant-assoc`             = ct$n_plant_assoc,

Neither grouping supports the predicted 'coprophilous more diffuse' direction. The full per-OTU × plant coefficient table (with Wald z, p and BH-q) is provided as tables/gllvm_H3_perOTU_plant_coef.csv.")
```

:::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
**Interpretation.** *\[To be written for the 2026-10 refit — Daniel.\]*
::::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
*Pre-refit interpretation (2026-07 models with six rank-3 genus predictors; superseded — kept for reference, its coprophile–Vaccinium result no longer holds):*

**Interpretation.** Two independent frameworks — a partial-pooling Bayesian joint model and an unpooled frequentist GLLVM — give the same answer: recognised coprophilous taxa are **not** more diffuse in their plant associations than other taxa, so H3 as preregistered is not supported, and the one robust piece of ecology (a positive coprophile–*Vaccinium* covariation, *Thelebolus* under one model, *Sporormiella* under the other) is the reverse of the ingested-passenger signature the test was built to detect. The two models disagree only on how many single-plant slopes count as "resolved," and that gap is exactly the expected footprint of shrinkage — the pooled model is conservative, the unpooled one liberal — not an ecological disagreement. Consistent with the forward-directional inference rule, neither the sparse Bayesian resolutions nor the plentiful GLLVM ones are read as evidence about gut residency; the honest reading remains that these winter-browse plants and the persistent dung-fungal core co-vary as parallel seasonal signatures, and that a larger, more diet-even matched sample is needed to test single-taxon passenger transport directly.
:::

## Section 8: Functional guilds — FUNGuild {.page-break-before}

:::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
Sections 3–6 characterise the seasonal shift *taxonomically* — which lineages turn over between winter and summer. This section asks what that community **does**: each OTU is assigned to a functional guild, and the guild composition of the dung mycobiome is compared across seasons. It is the descriptive counterpart to Section 9, which puts the same trait → season link inside a joint species distribution model. The two are deliberately built on the **same classification rule** so their results are directly comparable, but they differ in scope: Section 8 works on read shares across **all 1129 OTUs** of the canonical 52-sample object (no prevalence filter, because this is a description of where the reads go), whereas Section 9 models the 226 OTUs that pass its prevalence threshold. All results here are produced by `Scripts/8_functional_guilds.R`.
::::

Each OTU is assigned to a functional guild, and guild read shares are compared between seasons on all 1129 OTUs of the canonical object (no prevalence filter, since this describes where the reads go). Section 9 uses the same classification rule as a trait in the HMSC model, on the 226 OTUs that pass its prevalence filter. All results here come from `Scripts/8_functional_guilds.R`.

### 8.1 Guild assignment and the classification rule

Guild annotation uses **FUNGuild** (Nguyen et al. 2016), run through its command-line tool against each OTU's own taxonomy string, so that assignments are made at the finest rank available per OTU (species, genus, family or order) rather than by a single-rank lookup. **693 of the 1129 canonical OTUs (61.4%) receive a guild call** at a usable confidence ranking; the remaining 436 return no assignment — either because no matching taxonomy record exists in the FUNGuild database or because the match carries no ranked guild.

FUNGuild returns compound guild strings rather than a single label — for example `|Dung Saprotroph|-Endophyte-Plant Saprotroph-Undefined Saprotroph`. OTUs are collapsed to a single class by a priority rule (first match wins): dung saprotroph → plant-associated → pathotroph, with anything else falling to *other assigned* or *unassigned* (no FUNGuild call at all). Coprophily takes precedence: it is the guild the study is about, and it would otherwise be absorbed into a generic saprotroph category. An OTU counts as a dung saprotroph if FUNGuild lists `Dung Saprotroph` **or** its genus is one of the fourteen recognised coprophilous genera of Section 3.2. This is the identical rule used for the Section 9 guild trait.

```{r tab-guild-crosswalk}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
cw <- read.csv("tables/guild_scheme_crosswalk.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
lv <- c("Dung saprotroph", "Plant-associated", "Pathotroph",
        "Other assigned", "Unassigned / dark")
cw <- cw[order(match(cw$guild_display, lv)), ]
kable(data.frame(
  `Guild (Section 8)`      = cw$guild_display,
  `Class (Section 9)`     = cw$guild_class,
  `n OTUs`                 = cw$n_OTUs,
  Note                     = cw$note,
  check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Table S-GUILDa. Crosswalk between the Section 8 display guilds and the Section 9 model trait, with OTU counts (1129 canonical OTUs). The two schemes are the same priority rule; they differ only in that Section 9's `other` class is split here according to whether the OTU carries a FUNGuild annotation at all.")
```

### 8.2 Guild composition shifts sharply between seasons

![](figures/Fig1_guild_season.png)

**Figure S-GUILDa**: Functional-guild composition of the dung mycobiome. **(A)** Per-sample guild read share, one stacked bar per dung sample, faceted by season and ordered within each season by dung-saprotroph share. **(B)** Per-sample read share by guild and season; boxes show the median and interquartile range, points are individual samples, and marks give the Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted Wilcoxon rank-sum result (\* q \< 0.05, \*\* q \< 0.01, ns = not significant). **(C)** Mean guild read share by season and year, showing that the shift recurs in all three years. Colours are the Okabe–Ito colourblind-safe palette throughout.

Panel **(A)** here is the same object and rule as main-text **Fig. 1B** (Section 10.1) — the same result, not a second analysis. Panel **(B)** is the per-guild season test that the main text cites from here, and panel **(C)**, the Season × Year consistency check of Section 8.3, has no main-text counterpart.

:::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
The seasonal contrast is large and concerns primarily two of the five guilds. **Dung saprotrophs rise from 13.6% of winter reads to 51.5% in summer**, while the **unassigned/dark fraction falls from 51.1% to 21.0%** — that is, roughly half of a typical winter sample consists of reads that FUNGuild cannot place at all, whereas a typical summer sample is dominated by recognised coprophilous fungi. Equivalently, the proportion of reads landing on a guild-annotated OTU rises from **49% in winter to 79% in summer**.
::::

```{r tab-guild-season}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
g <- read.csv("tables/guild_season_readshare.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
pc <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f", 100 * x)
kable(data.frame(
  Guild            = g$Guild,
  `Summer mean %`  = pc(g$mean_summer),
  `Winter mean %`  = pc(g$mean_winter),
  `Summer median %`= pc(g$median_summer),
  `Winter median %`= pc(g$median_winter),
  `Detected (S/W)` = paste0(g$prevalence_summer, "/", g$prevalence_winter),
  `p`              = signif(g$p_value, 2),
  `q (BH)`         = ifelse(is.na(g$q_value), "—", signif(g$q_value, 2)),
  check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Table S-GUILDb. Per-sample guild read shares by season (26 samples per season), with Wilcoxon rank-sum tests and Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment across the five guilds. 'Detected' gives the number of samples in which the guild occurs at all. The final row is a robustness check, not part of the BH family: it restricts the dung-saprotroph guild to OTUs matching a recognised coprophilous genus, discarding those assigned on the FUNGuild string alone.")
```

**The dung-saprotroph result does not depend on how generously that guild is defined.** The rule counts an OTU as coprophilous if FUNGuild lists `Dung Saprotroph` *or* its genus is a recognised coprophilous genus. Restricting it to the genus criterion alone drops 24 of the 37 OTUs (37 across all 1129 canonical OTUs; the 14 dung saprotrophs of the Section 9 model are those of the 37 that pass its ≥ 5-replicate prevalence filter) and still gives **45.7% summer versus 8.5% winter** (p = 0.00094; final row of Table S-GUILDb). The signal is concentrated in a few abundant taxa — OTU1 (*Thelebolus*), OTU636 (*Sporormiella*) and OTU1225 (*Coniochaeta*) are the three largest contributors — which is consistent with the dominance analysis of Section 5.4 and with Section 9.4, where they are the three most summer-shifted OTUs of the HMSC model.

### 8.3 The guild shift recurs in all three years

```{r tab-guild-year}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
sy <- read.csv("tables/guild_season_year_readshare.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
lv <- c("Dung saprotroph", "Plant-associated", "Pathotroph",
        "Other assigned", "Unassigned / dark")
cells <- c("Winter 2022","Winter 2023","Winter 2024","Summer 2022","Summer 2023","Summer 2024")
sy$cell <- factor(paste(sy$Season, sy$Year), levels = cells)
mat <- tapply(sy$mean_share, list(factor(sy$Guild, levels = lv), sy$cell),
              function(z) z[1])
kable(cbind(Guild = lv, as.data.frame(round(100 * mat, 1), check.names = FALSE)),
      row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Table S-GUILDc. Mean per-sample guild read share (%) by season and year. Cell sizes: winter 10/9/7 and summer 9/9/8 samples for 2022/2023/2024.")
```

Panel C of Figure S-GUILDa and Table S-GUILDc show the same ordering in every year: **the dung-saprotroph share is higher in summer than in winter in 2022, 2023 and 2024** (41.3% vs 24.5%, 68.3% vs 10.9%, and 44.0% vs 1.7% respectively). Within-year tests are significant for 2023 (q = 0.027) and marginal for 2024 (q = 0.053) but not for 2022 (q = 0.74), where two unusually coprophile-rich winter samples raise the winter mean and its variance. The direction is therefore consistent across all three years while the magnitude varies.

:::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
This is the functional-guild analogue of the H1 result in Section 4.2, and the two agree closely: the compositional Season × Year interaction is significant there (p = 0.011; four of five distance measures, marginal under the fifth, Table S7b), and the per-year breakdown ranks the years in the same order as the guild data — 2023 strongest, 2024 intermediate, 2022 weakest (Table S5b). Given three years and modest per-cell sample sizes, the safe reading is that the seasonal shift is directionally reproducible but of year-varying magnitude, not that it has a constant effect size.
::::

::: {.callout-note when-profile="docs"}
**Interpretation and caveats.**

:::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
**What this adds.** The guild layer reproduces the seasonal signal independently of taxonomy and gives it a functional reading: summer dung supports an actively coprophilous community, winter dung does not. Section 9 tests the same link within a joint model and reaches a concordant conclusion — guild predicts seasonal *occurrence*, with dung saprotrophs more likely to occur in summer (posterior support 0.96) — so the descriptive and model-based views agree.
::::

**Relation to the dark taxa (E1).** The winter unassigned share here (51.1%) closely tracks the dark-taxa share reported in Section 3.4 (51.3% of winter reads), but the two are **not the same set**: "unassigned" here means no FUNGuild annotation (436 OTUs), while "dark" in Section 3.4 means no confident genus in the canonical taxonomy (493 OTUs). They share 390 OTUs, and 103 OTUs lack a genus yet still receive a FUNGuild call at family or order level. The definitions coincide in winter but diverge in summer (21.0% unassigned versus 31.2% dark), so the two figures should not be used interchangeably. Section 3.4 shows that much of this winter fraction is candidate-novel rather than merely unnamed; the functional consequence is that **winter guild composition is the least well characterised part of this dataset**, and its apparent depletion of coprophiles is partly a statement about annotation coverage.

**Limitations.** (i) Read share is not biomass: PCR and copy-number biases mean these proportions describe sequence abundance, not fungal abundance. (ii) FUNGuild assignments are database-derived and inherit its taxonomic and geographic biases; assignments made at family or order level are necessarily coarser than species-level ones, and confidence rankings (Table S-GUILDb does not stratify by them) are `Probable` for the majority of assigned OTUs. (iii) The compositional constraint discussed above means that a guild's decline in relative terms need not imply any absolute decline. (iv) A guild label describes an ecological capability inferred from relatives, not a verified activity in this substrate.
:::

#### Documentation notes — Section 8 {.unnumbered}

*Documentation build only; omitted from the submitted appendix. Move any paragraph, callout or table here that belongs in the full record rather than in the supplement.*

Section 9's residual `other` class mixes OTUs that *do* carry a FUNGuild call with 46 that have a taxonomic genus but **no** guild annotation at all; the latter carry roughly a tenth of winter reads. That conflation is harmless for a model trait but misleading in a read-share figure, so the two are separated here into **Other assigned** and folded into **Unassigned / dark** respectively. Table S-GUILDa reconciles the two schemes.

**Supersedes.** The preliminary guild percentages previously recorded in this section were an interim workspace check that predated the finalized script; they were not reproducible from any committed code. The values above are produced by `Scripts/8_functional_guilds.R` and are reproducible from the staged CSVs in `tables/`.

**Why FUNGuild and not FungalTraits.** Both annotation sources were built and compared. `fungaltraits_otu` (genus-level lookup via the `fungaltraits` package) covers 195 of 1129 OTUs (17%) and is a **strict subset** of the FUNGuild annotation (693 of the 1129 canonical OTUs, 61%) — it contributes no unique coverage. On the 195 OTUs both annotate they agree on the exact `Guild` string only 37% of the time (49% on trophic mode), because collapsing to one record per genus discards the species-level resolution FUNGuild's per-OTU run retains. FUNGuild is therefore used as the sole guild source; FungalTraits is retained only as a coarse sensitivity check, and guild calls are never merged between the two for the same OTU.

**Means and medians tell different parts of this story, and both are reported.** For the plant-associated and pathotroph guilds the seasonal *means* are nearly identical (18.0% vs 23.4%, and 4.7% vs 5.8%) while the *medians* differ several-fold (2.1% vs 18.4%, and 0.1% vs 3.8%). The rank-based tests follow the medians and are significant for both. The reason is compositional rather than ecological: because dung saprotrophs occupy so much of a typical summer sample, every other guild is compressed toward zero in most summer samples, while a small number of summer samples in which coprophiles are absent carry large plant-associated or pathotroph fractions and pull the summer means back up. These guilds are better described as **relatively displaced in summer** than as absolute winter specialists — a limitation inherent to read shares, which are constrained to sum to one.
:::

## Section 9: Joint species distribution model — HMSC (H1 synthesis) {.page-break-before}

:::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
Sections 4–6 treat the seasonal signal one lens at a time: community dissimilarity (H1), per-sample diversity (H2), and per-OTU differential abundance (GLLVM). This section brings them into a single hierarchical model. We fit a joint species distribution model (HMSC — Hierarchical Modelling of Species Communities; `Scripts/10_hmsc.R`) that simultaneously (i) partitions each OTU's variance among Season, Year, and the nested sampling structure; (ii) asks whether an OTU's functional guild predicts how it responds to Season (the trait → environment link); (iii) recovers each OTU's seasonal niche for a like-for-like cross-check against the Section-6 GLLVM; (iv) estimates the residual co-occurrence left once Season, Year and traits are accounted for; and (v) tests for phylogenetic signal in seasonal niches. It is the model-based synthesis of the H1 story, fitted directly on the corrected canonical data (unlike the Section-6 GLLVM, which predates the depth-filter fix).
::::

This section fits a joint species distribution model (HMSC; `Scripts/10_hmsc.R`) to the corrected canonical data. It partitions each OTU's variance among Season, Year and droppings (9.2), tests whether functional guild predicts the seasonal response (9.3), estimates each OTU's seasonal niche (9.4), residual co-occurrence (9.5) and phylogenetic signal (9.6), and reports predictive performance (9.7).

### 9.1 Model design and convergence

The models use the one-row-per-PCR-replicate object (`alldat_full$nopool`; 109 replicate rows from 55 biological dung samples), retaining the **226 OTUs present in ≥ 5 replicates** — the same prevalence rule used for the GLLVM/H3 analyses. Fixed effects are **Season** (winter as reference) **+ Year**; the species trait is the five-level functional **guild** class derived from FUNGuild (dung saprotroph, plant-associated, pathotroph, dark/unassigned, other — assigned by the priority rule in `Scripts/10_hmsc.R`, counts below). Three models are fitted:

- **Headline — CLR abundance, replicates averaged.** Each PCR replicate is CLR-transformed (the compositional normalisation that stands in for a library-size offset), and the two replicates of a dropping are then averaged, giving one row per dropping (55 rows). The random level is the **biological sample** (the dropping), with two latent factors. This model carries the abundance results of this section and all three panels of Figure 2.
- **Complement — CLR abundance, replicate level.** The same CLR response with both replicates kept as rows (109 rows), and **two random levels**: biological sample (two latent factors) and **PCR replicate** (one latent factor).
- **Robustness — presence/absence (probit)**, replicate level, with biological sample and PCR replicate as random levels.

Both CLR models scale each OTU's response to unit variance before fitting and cap the number of latent factors; the reason for the cap, and for the choice of headline, is given below Table S-HMSCb.

```{r tab-hmsc-guild}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
og <- read.csv("tables/hmsc_otu_guild.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
gt <- as.data.frame(table(factor(og$guild_class,
        levels = c("dung_saprotroph","plant_associated","pathotroph","dark_unassigned","other"))))
kable(data.frame(`Guild group` = gt$Var1, `n OTUs` = gt$Freq, check.names = FALSE),
      caption = "Table S-HMSCa. Functional-guild composition of the 226 modelled OTUs. FUNGuild returns a compound guild string per OTU; these are resolved to one class by the hierarchical priority rule in `Scripts/10_hmsc.R`, shared verbatim with Section 8. Dark/unassigned and 'other' together dominate the count — the modest coprophilous set (14 OTUs) nonetheless carries the strongest seasonal signal (Sections 9.3–9.4).")
```

An **individual-bird** random level was deliberately **not** included. Microsatellite genotyping succeeded for only a handful of repeat birds, so a bird level (with unidentified droppings entered as singletons) would have \~51 units against 55 biological samples — effectively one-to-one with the sample level, confounding the two sets of latent factors. In the three-level version this stopped the CLR community-level parameters from converging and made the variance partition unstable, so the bird level was dropped, leaving sample + PCR (mirroring the GLLVM's `(1 | Sample_ID_field)`). Dropping it was not by itself sufficient; see the note below Table S-HMSCb. Each model was fitted with four chains (1000 samples, thinning 50, 25,000 transient iterations).

```{r tab-hmsc-conv}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
cv <- read.csv("tables/hmsc_convergence_psrf.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
lab <- c(clr = "CLR abundance, replicates averaged (headline)",
         clr_rep = "CLR abundance, replicate level (complement)",
         pa = "Probit occurrence, replicate level", clr_phylo = "CLR + phylogeny")
kable(data.frame(
  Model = lab[cv$model], Rows = cv$n_rows,
  `Beta PSRF median / max` = sprintf("%.3f / %.3f", cv$beta_psrf_med, cv$beta_psrf_max),
  `Beta % < 1.1` = cv$beta_pct_below_1.1,
  `Season Beta % < 1.1` = cv$season_pct_below_1.1,
  `Gamma PSRF median / max` = sprintf("%.3f / %.3f", cv$gamma_psrf_med, cv$gamma_psrf_max),
  `Chain range, guild means` = cv$guild_mean_chain_range_max,
  `Chain range, variance partition` = cv$vp_chain_range_max,
  check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Table S-HMSCb. Convergence of the three HMSC models. PSRF is the Gelman–Rubin potential scale reduction factor (1 = the four chains agree). The two chain-range columns compare the chains directly on the quantities the figures report: the largest difference between chains in any guild's mean Season Beta (standardised units), and in any community-mean variance component (proportion).")
```

```{r tab-hmsc-v1}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
v1 <- read.csv("tables/hmsc_v1_chain_disagreement.csv", check.names = FALSE)
kable(v1, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("Quantity", "Chain 1", "Chain 2", "Chain 3", "Chain 4", "PSRF"),
      caption = "Table S-HMSCb2. An uncapped CLR model (replicate level; 7 latent factors at the sample level, 5 at the PCR level), shown for comparison. Each of its four chains converged to a different answer for the quantities Figure 2 reports, so pooling the chains gives a mixture of modes rather than an estimate.")
```

::: callout-note
**Why the latent factors are capped, and why the replicate-averaged model is the headline.** A CLR model at the replicate level with an uncapped number of latent factors (seven at the sample level, five at the PCR level) does not converge to one answer: its four chains settle in four different solutions (Table S-HMSCb2): the *Thelebolus* Season coefficient was 0.36, 3.03, 0.69 and −0.03 in the four chains, and the Season share of variance between 5% and 28%. The PSRF understated the problem because each chain mixed well within its own solution. The cause is structural. Season is constant within a dropping, so enough sample-level latent factors can reproduce the Season contrast themselves, and each chain divided the seasonal signal differently between the Season coefficients and the latent factors. Longer chains do not cure this; capping the number of latent factors does, and both CLR models reported here are capped.

With the cap, both CLR models converge on the Season effects (Table S-HMSCb). They differ in how they treat the two PCR replicates of each dropping. The replicate-level model estimates PCR replicate as its own random level, but the split of variance between dropping and replicate rests on only 54 replicate pairs and is weakly identified: in an earlier independent fit with the identical specification, its chains settled in two different splits (dropping/PCR 0.52/0.14 in two chains, 0.43/0.27 in the other two), whereas in the fit reported here the chains agree (Table S-HMSCc3). The replicate-level model also counts the two replicates as partly independent observations, which narrows its credible intervals (median width 0.84 of the headline model's; Table S-HMSCc4). Averaging the replicates removes both issues by construction — one row per dropping, no replicate-level split to identify — and its chains agree to within 0.003 on every reported guild mean and variance component.

The two models agree on what the figures report: per-OTU Season coefficients correlate at Pearson r = 0.97 (Spearman ρ = 0.89), and 56 OTUs have a 95% credible interval excluding zero in both (Table S-HMSCc4). The replicate-level model is therefore kept as the complement that carries an explicit PCR-replicate level, and the PCR-replicate variance the headline model averages away is measured directly in Section 9.2 (Table S-HMSCc2).

The **probit (occurrence)** model has low PSRFs (Beta median 1.01, 99.6% below 1.1), but compared chain by chain its guild means differ by up to 0.24 on the probit scale — the same qualitative answer in every chain, with looser agreement than the CLR models. That agreement is also partly a property of this particular fit: refitted from scratch, and again with its latent factors capped as in the CLR models, the same model mixes less well, with chains up to about 0.6 apart on a guild mean, chiefly for the common, strongly seasonal OTUs. Every refit returns the same answers — per-OTU Season coefficients correlate at r ≥ 0.99 with the fit reported here, and every guild-level direction is unchanged — so the probit results below should be read for their direction and ranking, not their exact size.
:::

### 9.2 Variance partitioning

For every OTU the headline model decomposes the variance it explains in CLR abundance into contributions from Season, Year, and the biological-sample (dropping) random level. Averaged across OTUs, **Season accounts for 31.5% and Year for 18.5%**, with the remaining 49.9% carried by differences among droppings. These are shares of the variance the model explains, not of total variance, so they are not comparable with a PERMANOVA R².

![](figures/hmsc_variance_partition.png)

**Figure S-HMSCa**: Per-OTU variance partitioning (CLR abundance, headline model). Each vertical bar is one OTU; colours give the proportion of that OTU's explained variance attributable to Season, Year and the biological-sample random level. Individual-dropping heterogeneity is the single largest component.

```{r tab-hmsc-vp}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
vp <- read.csv("tables/hmsc_variance_partition.csv", check.names = FALSE)
comp <- c("Season","Year","Random: sample")
cw  <- colMeans(vp[, comp])
byg <- aggregate(vp[, comp], list(Guild = vp$guild), mean)
tabb <- rbind(data.frame(Guild = "all OTUs (community mean)", t(cw), check.names = FALSE), byg)
tabb[, comp] <- round(tabb[, comp] * 100, 1)
pcr <- read.csv("tables/hmsc_pcr_replicate_variance.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
tabb$pcr <- round(100 * pcr$share_total_mean[match(sub("all OTUs \\(community mean\\)", "all", tabb$Guild), pcr$group)], 1)
kable(tabb, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("Guild group", "Season %", "Year %", "Dropping %", "PCR replicate % (model-free)"),
      caption = "Table S-HMSCc. Mean percentage of per-OTU variance attributed to each component of the headline model, community-wide and by guild; the three model components sum to 100%. The last column is not part of that partition: it is the model-free share of each OTU's total CLR variance that lies between the two PCR replicates of a dropping (Table S-HMSCc2).")
```

```{r tab-hmsc-pcr}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
pcr <- read.csv("tables/hmsc_pcr_replicate_variance.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
kable(data.frame(
  Group = pcr$group, `n OTUs` = pcr$n_otu,
  `Share of total variance, mean [95% CI]` = sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", pcr$share_total_mean,
                                                     pcr$boot_CrI2.5, pcr$boot_CrI97.5),
  `Median` = pcr$share_total_median,
  `Share after Season + Year` = pcr$share_resid_mean,
  `Mixed model (lme4)` = pcr$share_lme4_mean,
  `Detected in only one replicate` = pcr$discordance_mean,
  `Share when both replicates detect (median)` = pcr$share_both_median,
  check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Table S-HMSCc2. PCR-replicate variance, estimated outside the model from the 54 droppings with two replicates. For each OTU, replicate variance = mean(d²)/2, where d is the CLR difference between the two replicates; the share divides it by the OTU's total CLR variance and is averaged over OTUs (95% CI: 500 bootstrap resamples of droppings). Two cross-checks divide by the variance left after Season and Year, or take the residual share from a per-OTU mixed model with a dropping random intercept. 'Detected in only one replicate' is the fraction of droppings containing the OTU in which only one replicate detected it; the last column repeats the share using only droppings where both did. Per-OTU values: tables/hmsc_pcr_replicate_variance_perOTU.csv.")
```

```{r tab-hmsc-rep}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
vc <- read.csv("tables/hmsc_rep_vp_by_chain.csv", check.names = FALSE)
vc[, -1] <- round(100 * vc[, -1], 1)
kable(vc, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("Chain", "Season %", "Year %", "Dropping %", "PCR replicate %"),
      caption = "Table S-HMSCc3. Variance partition of the complementary replicate-level model (both PCR replicates as rows; dropping and PCR replicate as random levels), shown chain by chain.")
rv <- read.csv("tables/hmsc_rep_vs_main.csv")
kable(data.frame(
  `OTUs` = rv$n_otu, `Pearson r` = rv$pearson, `Spearman ρ` = rv$spearman,
  `CrI width, replicate-level / headline (median)` = rv$median_CrI_width_ratio_rep_over_main,
  `95% CrI excl. 0: headline / replicate-level / both` =
    sprintf("%d / %d / %d", rv$resolved95_main, rv$resolved95_rep, rv$resolved95_both),
  check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Table S-HMSCc4. Agreement between the headline and the replicate-level model on each OTU's Season coefficient (CLR units).")
```

:::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
The ecological reading is two-sided but coherent. The **seasonal axis is real and reproducible**, yet at the level of an individual OTU the largest single component is still *how much dung communities differ from one dropping to the next*. HMSC formalises what the ordination and dominance analyses already suggested: season shifts the community in a consistent direction, on top of large individual-level variability. This decomposition, broken down by guild exactly as in Table S-HMSCc, is Figure 2C of the main text (Section 10.2), for all OTUs, dung saprotrophs and unassigned / dark OTUs.
::::

**PCR-replicate variance.** Because the headline model averages the two PCR replicates of each dropping, it has no PCR level to partition. The replicate-to-replicate variance is measured instead, outside the model, from the 54 droppings with two replicates (Table S-HMSCc2). Both replicates come from the same DNA extract, so any difference between them is measurement noise. For each OTU, half the mean squared difference between the two replicates' CLR values estimates the replicate variance; divided by the OTU's total CLR variance and averaged over OTUs, **replicate noise accounts for 32% of CLR variance** (bootstrap 95% CI 28–40%; median over OTUs 25%). The estimate does not depend on the method: dividing instead by the variance left after Season and Year gives 36%, and a per-OTU mixed model with a dropping random intercept gives 34% (per-OTU correlation with the former 0.998). Nor is it driven by unequal sequencing depth: the two replicates differ in depth by a median factor of 1.31, and the size of that difference does not predict how different the replicates look (Spearman ρ = 0.21, p = 0.13, n = 54). It is not spread evenly, however. Coprophilous dung saprotrophs are the most repeatable guild (17%, CI 11–25%) and pathotrophs the least (50%, CI 36–62%).

The replicate noise is almost entirely **detection**, not abundance. Where both replicates detect an OTU, their CLR values agree closely: replicate noise is then a median 3% of variance. But in 46% of the droppings in which an OTU is found, only one of the two replicates detects it — the signature of low-abundance taxa near the detection limit, where PCR and sequencing sampling decide whether a few reads appear. Coprophiles are detected in both replicates more consistently (only one replicate detects them in 32% of cases) and, when both detect them, differ by a median 1% of variance: where *Thelebolus* or *Sporormiella* is present, both replicates see it at similar levels. The complementary replicate-level model, which fits PCR replicate as a random level, gives a comparable picture: 27% of its explained variance at the PCR level, 43% at the dropping level, and a Season share of 17.5% (Table S-HMSCc3). Its Season share is lower than the headline model's because replicate noise, which the headline model averages away, enters its denominator.

### 9.3 Guild as a predictor of the seasonal response (trait model)

The trait → environment matrix (Gamma) asks whether an OTU's guild predicts its seasonal response. Read from the probit occurrence model, it does. Relative to the winter reference, **dung saprotrophs are markedly more likely to occur in summer** (the reference-guild Season effect is positive with posterior support 0.96), and the yeast-rich "other" group shows the same direction (support 0.83); **pathotrophs lean the opposite way**, toward winter (support 0.85 in the negative direction). Plant-associated and dark/unassigned taxa show no clear guild-level seasonal preference.

![](figures/hmsc_probit_gamma.png)

**Figure S-HMSCb**: Trait → environment link (Gamma) from the probit occurrence model. Cells show the posterior support for each guild's response to Season and Year; the dung-saprotroph summer signal and the guild-structured Year (2024) shift are the supported effects. Red = positive (summer / higher), blue = negative.

```{r tab-hmsc-gamma}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
g <- read.csv("tables/hmsc_probit_gamma_CrI.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
g <- g[g$covariate == "Seasonsummer", ]
g$trait <- sub("^guild", "", g$trait)
g$trait[g$trait == "(Intercept)"] <- "dung saprotroph (reference)"
kable(data.frame(
  `Guild (trait)` = g$trait,
  `Gamma (summer)` = round(g$mean, 2),
  `95% CrI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", g$CrI_2.5, g$CrI_97.5),
  `Support P(>0)` = round(g$support, 2),
  check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Table S-HMSCd. Probit Gamma — guild trait → probability of summer occurrence. The reference row is the dung-saprotroph guild's own Season effect; the other rows are deviations from it. Support is the posterior probability that the coefficient exceeds zero (values near 1 = summer, near 0 = winter).")
```

```{r tab-hmsc-gamma-clr}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
g <- read.csv("tables/hmsc_gamma_CrI.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
g <- g[g$covariate == "Seasonsummer", ]
g$trait <- sub("^guild", "", g$trait)
g$trait[g$trait == "(Intercept)"] <- "dung saprotroph (reference)"
kable(data.frame(
  `Guild (trait)` = g$trait,
  `Gamma (summer)` = round(g$mean, 2),
  `95% CrI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", g$CrI_2.5, g$CrI_97.5),
  `Support P(>0)` = round(g$support, 3),
  check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Table S-HMSCd2. Abundance Gamma — guild trait → Season effect on CLR abundance, from the headline model, on the standardised scale (each OTU's response scaled to unit variance before fitting). Read as for Table S-HMSCd.")
```

On the abundance scale the same link can also be read from the headline model, whose Gamma converges (Table S-HMSCb), and it is sharper (Table S-HMSCd2). The dung-saprotroph guild's own Season effect is positive (+0.31 in standardised units, 95% CrI \[0.07, 0.54\], support 0.994). Plant-associated, pathotroph and dark/unassigned OTUs all respond clearly less summer-ward than dung saprotrophs (differences −0.37, −0.52 and −0.46; support ≤ 0.004), while the "other" group does not differ clearly from them (−0.16, support 0.12).

:::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
This is the guild-level counterpart to the taxonomic and dominance results (Sections 3.2, 5.4): the recognised coprophilous fungi — *Sporormiella*, *Thelebolus*, *Coniochaeta* — are not a fixed cold-adapted core but a **summer-occurring dung guild**, consistent with the richer, more fungal-propagule-laden summer diet. HMSC states that pattern as a trait effect estimated across all 226 OTUs at once, rather than genus by genus.
::::

### 9.4 Per-OTU seasonal niches, and agreement with the GLLVM

:::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
Extracting each OTU's Season coefficient (Beta) from the headline CLR model recovers the same lineages at the individual level. The **three most strongly summer-shifted OTUs are the coprophilous dung saprotrophs** *Thelebolus* (OTU1), *Sporormiella* (OTU636) and *Coniochaeta* (OTU1225), each with a 95% credible interval well clear of zero — while the **most strongly winter-shifted OTUs are dark/unassigned taxa**, led by OTU1369, the same taxonomically unresolved Dothideomycete that anchors winter dominance in Sections 5.4 and the E1 dark-taxa analysis (Section 3.4).
::::

Per-OTU Season coefficients from the headline model are ranked in Figure S-HMSCc and Tables S-HMSCe(i)–(ii). Figure S-HMSCg shows the 22 most abundant OTUs with their credible intervals, and main-text Figure 2A shows all 226 as one distribution.

![](figures/hmsc_beta_season.png)

**Figure S-HMSCc**: Per-OTU seasonal niche (HMSC CLR Beta on Season; positive = summer), for the 25 most summer- and 25 most winter-shifted OTUs, coloured by guild, with 95% credible intervals. The summer extreme is dominated by dung saprotrophs (warm) and yeasts; the winter extreme by dark/unassigned taxa. This is the same model and the same quantity as Figure S-HMSCg and main-text Figure 2A (Section 10.2), but selected differently: here the 50 most extreme OTUs are ranked by effect size, so the panel shows the community's extremes regardless of how rare they are, whereas Figure S-HMSCg restricts to the 22 OTUs holding at least 1% of modelled read share each and Figure 2A shows all 226 without intervals. Rare OTUs with large coefficients therefore appear here and not in Figure S-HMSCg.

```{r tab-hmsc-beta}
#| echo: false
suppressMessages(library(dplyr)); library(knitr)
b <- read.csv("tables/hmsc_beta_season.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
fmt <- function(d) d %>% transmute(
  OTU = OTU_ID, Genus = ifelse(is.na(Genus), "—", Genus), Guild = guild,
  Beta = round(beta_season_mean, 2),
  `95% CrI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", beta_season_CrI2.5, beta_season_CrI97.5),
  Support = round(beta_season_support, 2))
kable(b %>% arrange(desc(beta_season_mean)) %>% slice_head(n = 6) %>% fmt(), row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Table S-HMSCe(i). Most strongly summer-shifted OTUs (HMSC CLR Beta on Season).")
kable(b %>% arrange(beta_season_mean) %>% slice_head(n = 6) %>% fmt(), row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Table S-HMSCe(ii). Most strongly winter-shifted OTUs. Beta is in CLR units (the model's standardised coefficient multiplied by the OTU's CLR standard deviation). Full table: tables/hmsc_beta_season.csv.")
```

![](figures/S-HMSCg_top22_season_beta.png){width=80%}

**Figure S-HMSCg**: Season coefficient of the headline abundance (CLR) model, with 95% credible interval, for the 22 OTUs that each hold at least 1% of modelled read share (73% of modelled reads between them), coloured by functional guild; positive = more abundant in summer. Filled points are resolved at HMSC's 0.95 posterior-support convention (16 of 22). OTU1369's interval is clipped at −6 with an arrowhead (it reaches −6.48). The lower block gives the mean (diamond) and interquartile range of the per-OTU posterior means of each guild over all 226 OTUs. Figure S-HMSCc ranks the 50 most extreme OTUs instead, and main-text Figure 2A shows all 226.

```{r figS-hmscg-build}
#| eval: false
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Build code for Figure S-HMSCg — source of truth for figures/S-HMSCg_top22_season_beta.{png,pdf}"

# Figure S-HMSCg -- per-OTU Season coefficient for the 22 OTUs holding >= 1% of
# modelled read share, plus guild means (Section 9.4). Code carried over verbatim
# from the former main-text Figure 3A. Every number is READ from committed
# tables/ CSVs written by 10_hmsc.R and 9_dark_taxa_SH_matching.R.
# Rebuild:  conda run -n r_env Rscript build_main_figure.R figS-hmscg-build

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(ggplot2); library(patchwork); library(ggtext)
})

tab_dir <- if (dir.exists("tables")) "tables" else
           "/home/daniel/Ptarmigan/Scripts_server/Supplementary/tables"
out_dir <- "figures"
dir.create(out_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
grDevices::pdf(NULL)                                 # headless: no X11 fallback

# ---- shared style ----------------------------------------------------------
# Guild colours are Figure 1's, so a guild is the same colour in every main
# figure. The model's five-level trait is NOT identical to Figure 1's display
# split (46 OTUs move between "Other assigned" and "Unassigned / dark"); the
# caption says so and tables/guild_scheme_crosswalk.csv reconciles them.
GUILD_LEVELS <- c("Dung saprotroph", "Plant-associated", "Pathotroph",
                  "Other assigned", "Unassigned / dark")
guild_cols <- c("Dung saprotroph" = "#E69F00", "Plant-associated" = "#009E73",
                "Pathotroph" = "#CC79A7", "Other assigned" = "#56B4E9",
                "Unassigned / dark" = "#999999")
guild_map <- c(dung_saprotroph = "Dung saprotroph", plant_associated = "Plant-associated",
               pathotroph = "Pathotroph", other = "Other assigned",
               dark_unassigned = "Unassigned / dark")
# Variance components deliberately share NO colour with the guild scale, and
# split fixed (coloured) from random (grey): the visual point of panel B is how
# little of the bar is coloured.
# The headline model averages PCR replicates, so it has NO PCR random level;
# PCR-replicate variance is drawn as a separate, model-free column (panel B).
VP_LEVELS <- c("Season", "Year", "Random: sample")   # CSV column names
# Displayed names: the CSV's terse "Random: sample" is fine in a supplementary
# table but a main-text key has to say what the level actually is.
vp_display <- c("Season" = "Season", "Year" = "Year",
                "Random: sample" = "Biological sample (dropping)")
vp_cols <- c("Season" = "#0072B2", "Year" = "#F0E442",
             "Biological sample (dropping)" = "#666666")

base_theme <- theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text.y     = element_text(face = "bold", size = 8.5, angle = 0),
        plot.tag         = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
        plot.subtitle    = element_text(size = 9, colour = "grey30"),
        panel.spacing    = unit(0.5, "lines"),
        legend.key.size  = unit(0.42, "cm"),
        legend.title     = element_text(size = 10),
        legend.text      = element_text(size = 9))

# All in-plot text is ASCII: save_fig() falls back to grDevices::pdf when cairo
# is unavailable, and that device silently substitutes a dot for a Unicode glyph.
# (The markdown asterisks below are ggtext italics markup, and are ASCII.)

strip_rank <- function(x) sub("^[a-z]__", "", x)

# ============================================================================
# Panel A -- per-OTU seasonal niche (CLR abundance), plus guild means
# ============================================================================
b <- read.csv(file.path(tab_dir, "hmsc_beta_season.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
stopifnot(nrow(b) == 226L, !anyNA(b$beta_season_mean), !anyNA(b$beta_season_CrI2.5),
          !anyNA(b$beta_season_support), setequal(b$guild, names(guild_map)))
b$Guild <- factor(unname(guild_map[b$guild]), levels = GUILD_LEVELS)

# Read share AND full lineage both come from the E1 per-OTU table (Section 3.4),
# the one committed file carrying a complete Kingdom..Species lineage together
# with per-season mean read shares for every OTU in the study. Using it here is
# what lets an OTU with no genus be labelled by its finest resolved rank
# ("Dothideomycetes (OTU1369)") instead of a bare, unreadable ID.
sh <- read.csv(file.path(tab_dir, "dark_taxa_SH_matching.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
stopifnot(nrow(sh) == 1129L, all(b$OTU_ID %in% sh$OTU_ID), !any(duplicated(sh$OTU_ID)))
si <- match(b$OTU_ID, sh$OTU_ID)
# Guard: the Beta table's own Genus column must agree with the lineage source,
# or the labels would be describing different OTUs than the estimates.
stopifnot(all(is.na(b$Genus) == is.na(sh$Genus[si])),
          all(strip_rank(sh$Genus[si]) == b$Genus, na.rm = TRUE))

# winter_mean_share and summer_mean_share are each a mean over that season's
# samples, so their unweighted average is the OTU's mean share of a dropping.
# Renormalising over the 226 MODELLED OTUs (not all 1129) is what makes "1% of
# read share" a statement about the community the model actually sees.
b$share <- (sh$winter_mean_share[si] + sh$summer_mean_share[si]) / 2
stopifnot(!anyNA(b$share), all(b$share >= 0), sum(b$share) > 0)
b$rel <- b$share / sum(b$share)

# Selection rule: a stated threshold rather than an arbitrary top-N, so the
# panel's membership is reproducible and cannot be read as cherry-picked. It
# also ties this figure to main-text Figure 1, which is likewise read-share weighted.
SHARE_MIN <- 0.01
sel <- b[b$rel >= SHARE_MIN, ]
sel <- sel[order(-sel$beta_season_mean), ]
sel_cov <- sum(sel$rel)
stopifnot(nrow(sel) == 22L, sel_cov > 0.70, sel_cov < 0.76)

# Row labels: finest resolved rank, genus italicised via ggtext. Incertae sedis
# placeholders are not genera and are shown at the rank they actually resolve to.
RANKS <- c("Genus", "Family", "Order", "Class", "Phylum")
label_one <- function(i, otu) {
  v  <- strip_rank(unlist(sh[i, RANKS], use.names = FALSE))
  ok <- which(!is.na(v) & nzchar(v))
  if (!length(ok)) return(paste0("Fungi (", otu, ")"))
  k <- ok[1]
  nm <- sub("_(gen|fam|ord|cls)_Incertae_sedis$", "", v[k])
  if (k == 1L && !grepl("Incertae", v[k], fixed = TRUE)) nm <- paste0("*", nm, "*")
  paste0(nm, " (", otu, ")")
}
sel$lab <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(sel)),
                  function(j) label_one(match(sel$OTU_ID[j], sh$OTU_ID), sel$OTU_ID[j]),
                  character(1))
stopifnot(!any(duplicated(sel$lab)))

# Resolution marker: HMSC's own convention -- one-sided posterior support of
# 0.95, i.e. a 90% two-sided interval. The caption also reports how many OTUs
# community-wide have a 95% CrI excluding zero, so the weaker criterion is not
# passed off as the stronger.
SUPP <- 0.95
sel$resolved <- factor(
  ifelse(sel$beta_season_support >= SUPP | sel$beta_season_support <= 1 - SUPP,
         "Posterior support >= 0.95", "Not resolved"),
  levels = c("Posterior support >= 0.95", "Not resolved"))
n_res <- sum(sel$resolved == "Posterior support >= 0.95")

# Guild means over ALL OTUs of that guild (not just the 22 plotted), with the
# IQR of the same per-OTU estimates as a spread -- a summary of the points
# above, NOT a credible interval, which is why it is drawn as a plain segment.
gm <- do.call(rbind, lapply(GUILD_LEVELS, function(g) {
  v <- b$beta_season_mean[b$Guild == g]
  data.frame(Guild = factor(g, levels = GUILD_LEVELS), n = length(v),
             mean = mean(v), q25 = quantile(v, 0.25), q75 = quantile(v, 0.75),
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}))
gm$lab <- sprintf("%s (n = %d)", as.character(gm$Guild), gm$n)

# Drift guard against the committed per-OTU table itself -- guild sizes and
# guild means -- which is what the panel actually draws. (These are means of
# per-OTU posterior means in CLR units, NOT the trait-level Gamma, which is on
# the standardised scale and reported in Section 9.3.)
N_EXP  <- c("Dung saprotroph" = 14L, "Plant-associated" = 50L, "Pathotroph" = 16L,
            "Other assigned" = 67L, "Unassigned / dark" = 79L)
GM_EXP <- c("Dung saprotroph" = 1.320, "Plant-associated" = -0.095, "Pathotroph" = -0.332,
            "Other assigned" = 0.223, "Unassigned / dark" = -0.312)
gm_n <- setNames(gm$n, as.character(gm$Guild))
gm_m <- setNames(gm$mean, as.character(gm$Guild))
stopifnot(sum(N_EXP) == 226L, all(gm_n[names(N_EXP)] == N_EXP),
          max(abs(gm_m[names(GM_EXP)] - GM_EXP)) < 0.01,
          as.character(gm$Guild[which.max(gm$mean)]) == "Dung saprotroph")

# One plot, two blocks: facet_grid with free space gives the guild block a
# height proportional to its 5 rows and keeps ONE shared x axis and one tag.
BLOCKS <- c("Per-OTU niche", "Guild mean")   # short: the lower block is only 5 rows tall
otu_df <- data.frame(lab = sel$lab, Guild = sel$Guild, resolved = sel$resolved,
                     est = sel$beta_season_mean,
                     lo = sel$beta_season_CrI2.5, hi = sel$beta_season_CrI97.5,
                     block = factor(BLOCKS[1], levels = BLOCKS))
gm_df  <- data.frame(lab = gm$lab, Guild = gm$Guild, est = gm$mean,
                     lo = gm$q25, hi = gm$q75,
                     block = factor(BLOCKS[2], levels = BLOCKS))
lvl <- c(gm_df$lab[order(gm_df$est)], otu_df$lab[order(otu_df$est)])
otu_df$lab <- factor(otu_df$lab, levels = lvl)
gm_df$lab  <- factor(gm_df$lab,  levels = lvl)

# Convergence is checked here but PRINTED IN THE CAPTION, not on the panel: a
# diagnostic belongs in the caption rather than on the face of a main-text
# figure. The guard refuses to draw the figure from a fit that does not meet
# the Section 9.1 criteria (every Beta PSRF < 1.1; chains agree on the guild
# means and the variance partition to within 0.05).
conv <- read.csv(file.path(tab_dir, "hmsc_convergence_psrf.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
cclr <- conv[conv$model == "clr", ]
stopifnot(nrow(cclr) == 1L, cclr$beta_psrf_max < 1.1, cclr$beta_pct_below_1.1 == 100,
          cclr$guild_mean_chain_range_max < 0.05, cclr$vp_chain_range_max < 0.05)
n_ci <- sum(b$beta_season_CrI2.5 > 0 | b$beta_season_CrI97.5 < 0)
stopifnot(n_ci == 74L)

# OTU1369's credible interval reaches below -6; drawn in full it would widen
# the axis for one row. Intervals are therefore clipped at +/- 6 and the
# clipped end carries an arrowhead, so nothing is hidden: the reader sees that
# the interval continues, and the caption says how far.
XCLIP <- 6
otu_df$lo_c <- pmax(otu_df$lo, -XCLIP)
otu_df$hi_c <- pmin(otu_df$hi,  XCLIP)
otu_df$lo_clip <- otu_df$lo < -XCLIP
otu_df$hi_clip <- otu_df$hi >  XCLIP
n_clip <- sum(otu_df$lo_clip | otu_df$hi_clip)
# Nothing may be clipped so hard that its point estimate leaves the panel.
stopifnot(all(abs(otu_df$est) < XCLIP), all(abs(gm_df$est) < XCLIP),
          all(abs(c(gm_df$lo, gm_df$hi)) < XCLIP))
arr <- grid::arrow(length = unit(0.055, "in"), type = "open", angle = 22)

pA <- ggplot(otu_df, aes(est, lab, colour = Guild)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey70") +
  # geom_segment rather than geom_errorbarh: the latter is deprecated in
  # ggplot2 4.0 and its replacement's argument names differ between versions.
  geom_segment(aes(x = lo_c, xend = hi_c, y = lab, yend = lab), linewidth = 0.45, alpha = 0.75) +
  # Arrowheads drawn as short overlays at the clipped ends rather than as an
  # arrow on the main segment, so an interval clipped at BOTH ends still gets
  # two heads and an unclipped one gets none.
  geom_segment(data = otu_df[otu_df$hi_clip, ],
               aes(x = XCLIP - 0.30, xend = XCLIP, y = lab, yend = lab),
               linewidth = 0.45, alpha = 0.75, arrow = arr) +
  geom_segment(data = otu_df[otu_df$lo_clip, ],
               aes(x = -XCLIP + 0.30, xend = -XCLIP, y = lab, yend = lab),
               linewidth = 0.45, alpha = 0.75, arrow = arr) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = resolved), size = 2.3, stroke = 0.8) +
  # guild block: IQR segment behind, mean diamond on top, value printed
  geom_segment(data = gm_df, aes(x = lo, xend = hi, y = lab, yend = lab),
               inherit.aes = FALSE, colour = "grey65", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(data = gm_df, aes(est, lab, fill = Guild), inherit.aes = FALSE,
             shape = 23, size = 3.2, colour = "grey20", stroke = 0.4) +
  # Value printed to the RIGHT of the IQR, not above the diamond: the five guild
  # means sit within 0.6 of each other, so a label above one row lands on the next.
  geom_text(data = gm_df, aes(hi, lab, label = sprintf("%+.2f", est)), inherit.aes = FALSE,
            hjust = 0, nudge_x = 0.10, size = 2.9, colour = "grey20") +
  facet_grid(rows = vars(block), scales = "free_y", space = "free_y", switch = "y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = guild_cols, name = "Guild", drop = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = guild_cols, guide = "none", drop = FALSE) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Posterior support >= 0.95" = 16, "Not resolved" = 1),
                     name = NULL, drop = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-6, 6, 2), expand = expansion(mult = c(0.03, 0.09))) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-XCLIP, XCLIP)) +
  labs(x = "HMSC Beta: Season (CLR abundance)\npositive = more abundant in summer", y = NULL,
       subtitle = sprintf(paste0("The %d OTUs holding >= %.0f%% of modelled read share each (%.0f%% of modelled reads).\n",
                                 "Abundance (CLR) model; %d of %d resolved at 0.95 posterior support."),
                          nrow(sel), 100 * SHARE_MIN, 100 * sel_cov, n_res, nrow(sel))) +
  base_theme +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_markdown(size = 8.5),
        strip.placement = "outside",
        strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 90, face = "bold", size = 8)) +
  # Each panel carries its own key directly beneath it (not collected across the
  # figure), so a reader never has to work out which panel a key belongs to.
  guides(colour = guide_legend(order = 1, nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE, title.position = "top",
                               override.aes = list(shape = 16, size = 2.6)),
         shape  = guide_legend(order = 2, nrow = 1, title = "Resolution",
                               title.position = "top"))


pS <- pA + theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.box = "vertical",
                 legend.box.just = "left", legend.margin = margin(0, 0, 0, 0))
png(file.path(out_dir, "S-HMSCg_top22_season_beta.png"), width = 7.2, height = 7.4,
    units = "in", res = 300); print(pS); invisible(dev.off())
grDevices::cairo_pdf(file.path(out_dir, "S-HMSCg_top22_season_beta.pdf"), width = 7.2, height = 7.4)
print(pS); invisible(dev.off())
cat(sprintf("%d OTUs at >= %.0f%% modelled read share = %.1f%% of modelled reads; %d resolved.\n",
            nrow(sel), 100 * SHARE_MIN, 100 * sel_cov, n_res))
```

The same per-OTU niche can be estimated on the **occurrence** scale, with the probit model. There, 55 of the 226 OTUs have a Season coefficient whose 95% credible interval excludes zero, against 74 in the headline abundance model. The two formulations rank the community's seasonal responses consistently (Spearman ρ = 0.76), and the probit per-OTU estimates aggregate to the guild-level Gamma of Section 9.3 to within 0.04, so nothing here contradicts the results above. What the occurrence scale does change is *which* taxa sit at the summer extreme. In abundance the coprophiles lead outright; in occurrence the shift is community-wide (157 of 226 OTUs point towards summer, median +0.70) and the extreme is occupied by cold-adapted basidiomycete yeasts — *Vishniacozyma*, *Mrakia*, *Piskurozyma*, *Phenoliferia* — with *Sporormiella* (OTU636) the only dung saprotroph in the top 25 and the mean dung-saprotroph rank falling to 125 of 226 (from 59 in abundance). The distinction is ecologically substantive rather than a modelling artefact: coprophilous fungi are what summer dung is largely *made of* in read share, but they are not the taxa that most reliably *appear* in summer. The winter extreme is unchanged and, if anything, more strongly resolved — dark/unassigned taxa and pathotrophs, with OTU1369 the most winter-shifted OTU in the community (β = −2.25, 95% CrI \[−3.53, −1.08\]).

:::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
Both scales are carried forward, but they are not given equal weight in the main text. Figure 2 in Section 10.2 is built entirely on the abundance formulation — the scale on which the coprophilous shift is the community's largest seasonal effect, and the scale that Figure 1 also works on — while the occurrence-scale result reported here stays supplementary, alongside Tables S-HMSCe(iii) and S-HMSCe(iv). The abundance-scale table above also remains the one comparable with the GLLVM below.
::::

```{r tab-hmsc-beta-probit}
#| echo: false
suppressMessages(library(dplyr)); library(knitr)
bp <- read.csv("tables/hmsc_probit_beta_season.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
fmtp <- function(d) d %>% transmute(
  OTU = OTU_ID, Genus = ifelse(is.na(Genus), "—", Genus), Guild = guild,
  Beta = round(beta_season_mean, 2),
  `95% CrI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", beta_season_CrI2.5, beta_season_CrI97.5),
  Support = round(beta_season_support, 3))
kable(bp %>% arrange(desc(beta_season_mean)) %>% slice_head(n = 6) %>% fmtp(), row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Table S-HMSCe(iii). Most strongly summer- and winter-shifted OTUs on the occurrence scale (HMSC probit Beta on Season; positive = more likely to occur in summer). 55 of 226 OTUs have a 95% credible interval excluding zero. Full table: tables/hmsc_probit_beta_season.csv.")
kable(bp %>% arrange(beta_season_mean) %>% slice_head(n = 6) %>% fmtp(), row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Table S-HMSCe(iv). Most strongly winter-shifted OTUs, occurrence scale. Support is the posterior probability that the coefficient exceeds zero.")
```

Because the GLLVM (Section 6) is an independent model — negative-binomial counts rather than CLR abundance, a different random-effect structure, and fitted on a different OTU snapshot — the two provide a cross-method check. Their per-OTU Season coefficients agree well.

![](figures/hmsc_vs_gllvm_season.png)

**Figure S-HMSCd**: HMSC (CLR Beta) versus GLLVM Season coefficient, one point per shared OTU (n = 139 after excluding the GLLVM's on/off near-separation OTUs, whose ±10³ coefficients are not comparable), coloured by guild. The two independent joint models rank the OTUs' seasonal responses consistently (**Spearman ρ = 0.75**).

### 9.5 Residual co-occurrence beyond Season

The biological-sample latent factors capture the co-occurrence structure that remains once Season, Year and guild are accounted for — pairs of OTUs that rise and fall together across droppings for reasons the fixed effects do not explain.

![](figures/hmsc_omega_sample.png)

**Figure S-HMSCe**: Residual OTU–OTU association matrix (biological-sample level), showing only associations supported at ≥ 0.95 posterior probability and restricted to OTUs with at least one such association, ordered by hierarchical clustering. Red = positive residual co-occurrence, blue = negative. Blocks of positively associated OTUs indicate sub-communities that track together beyond the seasonal signal — candidate co-dispersed or co-sourced groups for follow-up.

### 9.6 Phylogenetic signal in seasonal niches

Adding the OTU phylogeny (the maximum-likelihood ITS2 tree of `Scripts/6_diversity_analyses.R`, pruned to the 226 modelled OTUs and rooted on the stem of Ascomycota, which forms a single clade in the tree) to the headline model estimates ρ: the share of the OTU-to-OTU variation in responses, left after the guild trait, that follows the phylogeny under a Brownian-motion model. The chains converge and agree on ρ (Table S-HMSCb, Table S-HMSCf), and adding the phylogeny leaves the per-OTU niches and the guild link essentially unchanged.

```{r tab-hmsc-rho}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
rh <- read.csv("tables/hmsc_rho_phylo.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
kable(data.frame(
  `ρ (median)` = round(rh$median, 3),
  `95% CrI` = sprintf("[%.3f, %.3f]", rh$CrI_2.5, rh$CrI_97.5),
  `P(ρ>0)` = rh$P_gt0, ESS = rh$ess, PSRF = round(rh$psrf, 3),
  `Chain medians` = rh$rho_chain_medians,
  check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = sprintf("Table S-HMSCf. Phylogenetic signal parameter ρ from the phylogeny-augmented version of the headline CLR model (same data and structure). ρ is sampled on a grid with steps of 0.005 from 0.905 to 0.995 and 0.05 below; the prior keeps HMSC's usual 0.5 point mass at ρ = 0 and spreads the rest uniformly over (0, 1). Adding the phylogeny leaves the per-OTU niches and trait link essentially unchanged (Season Beta / Gamma correlation with the headline model %.2f / %.2f).",
                    rh$beta_season_cor_vs_main, rh$gamma_cor_vs_main))
```

**ρ is effectively 1.** Its posterior median is 0.990 (95% CrI \[0.955, 0.995\]), and the posterior rises steadily toward the top of the grid, with a third of all draws on its highest point. That upper limit is set by the grid, not the data: ρ = 1 itself cannot be fitted, because OTUs with near-identical sequences have near-zero branch lengths and the phylogenetic covariance becomes singular. Under the model, essentially all of the variation in responses left after guild is phylogenetically structured. Note that ρ applies to an OTU's responses jointly — baseline abundance, Season and Year together.

:::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
**Tree rooting corrected (2026-11-18, branch `exp/hmsc-phylo-root`).** The ML tree is unrooted. The earlier fit (2026-10-01) was meant to root it, but the rooting step never ran, so the root fell wherever the tree-building software left it: between 12 Helotiales OTUs and the other 214, with Basidiomycota nested inside Ascomycota. Because HMSC's phylogenetic correlation matrix depends on the root when the tree is not ultrametric (root-to-tip depths 0.10–2.46 here), the tree is now rooted on the Ascomycota stem: Ascomycota (144 OTUs) against the other 82 (Basidiomycota 78, one Chytridiomycota, one *Mucor* placed inside Basidiomycota, and two phylum-unassigned OTUs). The correlation matrix changes substantially (off-diagonal r = 0.15 with the old one), but the answer barely moves: ρ was 0.985 (95% CrI \[0.950, 0.995\]) with a quarter of draws on 0.995, and is now 0.990 (\[0.955, 0.995\]) with a third there; the Gamma correlation with the headline model rose from 0.87 to 0.89, and the Season Beta of the two phylogeny fits correlate at 0.994. Close to ρ = 1 the model approaches Brownian motion with an estimated mean, whose likelihood hardly depends on where the root sits, so the correction removes a methodological weakness rather than changing the result. Same data, grid, prior, MCMC length and seeds; every other table in Section 9 is unchanged. Midpoint rooting was rejected because here it roots on the two long-branched phylum-unassigned OTUs.
::::

A single ρ does not say at which scale relatives resemble each other, and it does not isolate Season. Table S-HMSCf2 therefore correlates the Season responses of every pair of OTUs, binned by their distance in the tree. It uses the headline model's coefficients, which contain no phylogeny, so the comparison is not circular.

```{r tab-hmsc-correlogram}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
cg <- read.csv("tables/hmsc_phylo_season_correlogram.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
kable(data.frame(
  `Tree distance (subst./site)` = cg$distance_class,
  `OTU pairs` = format(cg$n_pairs, big.mark = ","),
  `Correlation of Season responses` = sprintf("%.2f", cg$r),
  `Range expected by chance (95%)` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", cg$null_2.5, cg$null_97.5),
  p = ifelse(cg$p_two_sided < 0.002, "< 0.002", sprintf("%.3f", cg$p_two_sided)),
  check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = sprintf("Table S-HMSCf2. Phylogenetic correlogram of seasonal responses. All %s pairs of the 226 modelled OTUs are binned by patristic distance in the ML tree (expected substitutions per site); within each bin, the two OTUs' standardised Season coefficients from the headline model are correlated (symmetric pairwise correlation). The chance range and p come from 500 permutations of OTU labels over the tree. Nothing is excluded: the %d OTUs with a neighbour within 0.005 are kept.",
                    format(sum(cg$n_pairs), big.mark = ","), cg$n_otu_with_neighbour_le_0.005[1]))
```

Close relatives respond alike, and the resemblance reaches well beyond near-identical sequences. The 27 pairs within 0.005 substitutions per site correlate at 0.82, pairs up to 0.1 at 0.63–0.65, and the 1,283 pairs at 0.1–0.5 — roughly genus-to-family distance — still at 0.40, each far above the range expected by chance. The resemblance fades by 0.5–1 (0.08) and reverses at the deepest splits (−0.10): the most distant lineages tend to respond to season in opposite directions. Near-identical sequences therefore do not drive the signal — they are 27 of about 25,000 pairs — and they are retained: they survived LULU curation, which merges a sequence into a close relative only when the two co-occur, so they are distinct units rather than sequencing duplicates.

The deep end of the correlogram needs a separate check. A tree built from ITS2 alone resolves recent splits well but places classes and phyla poorly, so the negative correlation at the largest distances rests on weak branches. Grouping the same Season responses by taxonomy instead, with no tree involved, shows the contrast directly (Table S-HMSCf3). Basidiomycota lean summer (72% of OTUs summer-positive), driven by the yeast classes Tremellomycetes and Microbotryomycetes. Ascomycota lean winter (43% summer-positive), driven by Dothideomycetes, Eurotiomycetes and Lecanoromycetes, the last two with only about one OTU in six summer-positive. Sordariomycetes, which include *Coniochaeta*, are the summer-leaning exception among Ascomycota.

```{r tab-hmsc-lineage}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
ln <- read.csv("tables/hmsc_season_by_lineage.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
kable(data.frame(
  Rank = ln$rank, Lineage = ln$lineage, `OTUs` = ln$n_otu,
  `Mean Season response (std.)` = sprintf("%+.2f", ln$mean_std_season_beta),
  `% summer-positive` = sprintf("%.0f%%", ln$pct_summer_positive),
  p = ifelse(ln$p_perm < 0.001, "< 0.001", sprintf("%.3f", ln$p_perm)),
  check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Table S-HMSCf3. Seasonal response by phylum and class, from taxonomy rather than the tree. For each lineage with at least four modelled OTUs: the mean standardised Season coefficient of the headline model (positive = summer), the percentage of its OTUs with a positive coefficient, and a permutation p (2000 random groups of the same size: is the lineage's mean further from the community mean than chance?). 'unassigned' = OTUs with a phylum but no class.")
```

Summer libraries are deeper than winter ones (Section 5.1), and a CLR value depends on read depth through its zeros, so the lineage pattern was re-estimated with depth controlled (Table S-HMSCf4). Simple per-OTU regressions on the same response reproduce the HMSC coefficients (r = 0.985). Adding each dropping's log library depth as a covariate, or first rarefying every PCR replicate to 20,000 reads (47 droppings), strengthens the basidiomycete summer lean (83% and 79% summer-positive) but removes the ascomycete lean at phylum level (54% and 53%). The winter lean holds only within particular ascomycete classes: Lecanoromycetes (17% summer-positive under every analysis), Eurotiomycetes (17–25%) and, more weakly, Dothideomycetes (45–47%).

```{r tab-hmsc-lineage-depth}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
ld <- read.csv("tables/hmsc_season_by_lineage_depth.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
pc <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", x)
kable(data.frame(
  Rank = ld$rank, Lineage = ld$lineage, OTUs = ld$n_otu,
  HMSC = pc(ld$pct_pos_hmsc), `Linear model` = pc(ld$pct_pos_lm),
  `+ log depth` = pc(ld$pct_pos_lm_logdepth), `Rarefied (20,000 reads)` = pc(ld$pct_pos_rarefied),
  check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = sprintf("Table S-HMSCf4. Depth check on Table S-HMSCf3: percentage of each lineage's OTUs with a summer-positive Season response. HMSC = headline model (as in Table S-HMSCf3). The other columns are per-OTU linear models of the same standardised, dropping-averaged CLR response on Season + Year (correlation with the HMSC coefficients across OTUs r = %.3f); the same with the dropping's log mean library depth added (r = %.2f); and Season + Year after rarefying each PCR replicate to 20,000 reads, dropping replicates below that (%d droppings kept), recomputing CLR and averaging per dropping, mean of 10 draws (r = %.2f).",
                    ld$r_lm_vs_hmsc[1], ld$r_logdepth_vs_hmsc[1], ld$n_drop_rarefied[1], ld$r_rarefied_vs_hmsc[1]))
```

Seasonal niches are **phylogenetically conserved**, most clearly at the genus-to-family scale, with the deepest lineages contrasting. It is reported as a secondary, exploratory result: the phylogeny-augmented model is a supplementary variant, and ρ at the upper edge of its range is better read as "strongly structured" than as a precise value.

:::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
This dovetails with the guild result — because guild is itself partly phylogenetically structured, the coprophilous summer signature is echoed as a broader phylogenetic pattern.
::::

### 9.7 Predictive performance

Finally, HMSC quantifies how much of the community it actually explains, in-sample versus out-of-sample (two-fold cross-validation, with folds split by biological sample so PCR replicates never leak across folds).

![](figures/hmsc_R2_explanatory_vs_cv.png)

**Figure S-HMSCf**: Explanatory (in-sample) versus two-fold cross-validated per-OTU R² for the CLR model. Points lie far below the 1:1 line: the model fits the observed communities well but does not predict held-out droppings.

```{r tab-hmsc-r2}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
r2 <- read.csv("tables/hmsc_predictive_R2_summary.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
lab <- c(clr = "CLR (abundance)", pa = "Probit (occurrence)")
kable(data.frame(
  Model = lab[r2$model],
  `Explanatory R²` = round(r2$mean_expl_R2, 3),
  `2-fold CV R²` = ifelse(is.na(r2$mean_cv_R2), "—", round(r2$mean_cv_R2, 3)),
  check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Table S-HMSCg. Community-mean explanatory vs cross-validated fit. Explanatory R² is moderate; cross-validated R² is near zero.")
```

The explanatory fit is moderate (community-mean R² ≈ 0.29 for the headline abundance model) but **cross-validated R² is near zero** (≈ 0.03) — the model does not predict the fungal community of a dropping it has not seen. The seasonal and guild effects documented above are **real and directional but small against the dominant, idiosyncratic variation among individual droppings**.

:::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
A ptarmigan's dung mycobiome is shaped by season in a reproducible way, yet remains largely individual — which is exactly what a transient, diet- and propagule-sourced community should look like, and a useful caution for anyone hoping to read season directly off a single sample.
::::

:::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
**In summary**, HMSC does not overturn any earlier result; it unifies them and adds two things the single-lens analyses could not: a variance decomposition that sizes the seasonal signal against individual heterogeneity, and a formal trait- and phylogeny-level account of *why* the seasonal turnover looks the way it does — a summer-occurring coprophilous dung guild, phylogenetically conserved, riding on top of large among-individual variability.
::::
